<header>Preface.</header>

than GOD, as the Jews also surmised of the Lord Christ, and said: That must be from the Devil. He has not studied the Scripture; where does he get the knowledge and the great power from? Just so we say, too. At the universities one studies, they know the way of GOD correctly; that is a "saint-eater" <note>an epithet for one who acts holier-than-thou</note>, he wants to be something special; what the enthusiast <term>Schwermer</term> <gloss>fanatic/enthusiast</gloss> says, there is no need to pay attention to. If GOD wants me pious, He will make me pious when the time comes that I should die; I will still turn then. Why should I make my heart heavy for long? I will be merry as long as I live; I get nothing out of it in the end. I know well what I have, but not what I will get; that I will first experience well then. GOD is gracious and merciful, He will have mercy on me. But hear! What does GOD's word say to this, and our Lord Christ in his Holy Gospel? Whoever wants to follow me, let him take up his cross and follow me: Repent and believe the Gospel: No one can serve two masters: My kingdom is not of this world: Here you have fear, but there your sadness shall be turned into joy, and other such heartfelt sayings more. Are these all also Weigelian, Schwenckfeldian, enthusiastic, Socinian, Quaker-like? For many a pious, honest man has not seen a letter of the writings of Weigel, Schwenckfeld, and others of the sort in his whole life, much less read them, yet he must let himself be

auch selbst ein exemplarisch Leben / gehe deinen Zu-
hörern mit guten Exempeln vor / so hastu ein gut
Gewissen / und gehen dich diese Reden ganz nichts
an / ja sprechen sie / thut nach meinen Worten und
nicht nach meinen Wercken / dadurch geben sie
zwar zu verstehen / daß sie rechte Phariseer seyn/
weilen sie sich dessen bedienen/ was der HErr Chri-
stus von ihnen gesagt: Nemlich; 
> Was sie euch sagen/ das thut / aber nach ihren Wercken solt ihr nicht thun.

Solche gottlose Geistliche werden aber auch am jüngsten Tage wiederum müssen hören / was dort der HErr Christus sagt: 
> Weichet von mir ihr Ubelthäter : 

Ob sie gleich werden sagen: 
> HERR haben wir nicht in deinen Namen geprediget / Kinder getauffet / das H. Abendmahl gereichet/ etc. 

Dann es muß so wohl Lehrer als Zuhörer / eine fruchtbare Rebe an dem Weinstocke Christi seyn / und die Prediger eben auch in Christo ein recht Christlich Leben führen/ damit sie nicht / wie der H. Apostel Paulus sagt: 
> andern Predigen und selbst verwerfflich werden/ 

sonst wird sie ihr Lehren und Predigen nichts helf-
fen/ wie können die Zuhörer Geistlich gelehret wer-
den / so die Prediger ein ungeistlich Leben führen/
werden sie sich nicht höchlich dran ärgern und sagen:
unser Pfarrherr thut das auch / ob gleich Gottes
Wort und Sacramenta in ihren Kräfften ver-
bleiben. Mein lieber Christ sage mir doch: Ob das

Ewigkeit bleiben müssen. **GOTT** gibt uns nicht
allein fromme Prediger / die uns zur Busse ver-
mahnen und das ihrige gnugsam thun / sondern
erwecket auch aus den einfältigen Läyen / die uns
den Weg zur Busse vorstellen müssen / und wann
die nicht wären / so müßten es die Steine auff Got-
tes Befehl verrichten / ob wir uns von Hertzen zu
Ihm bekehren wollen / so hat Gott seine Hand aus-
gestreckt den gantzen Tag / uns mit Freuden zu em-
pfahen / da dann Freud im Himmel soll seyn / über
einen Sünder der Busse thut ; Aber leyder! nie-
mand / niemand läst unser Predigt zu Ohren kom-
men / sondern predige uns fein sanffte / das uns
wohl thue / das haben wir gerne / das Hertz bleibet
in den Irrdischen verwircket / kan nicht loß werden /
dann es ist der Sünden Knecht / begehret nicht frey
zu seyn / die alte Gewohnheit will sich nicht ändern
lassen / wir wolten gerne alle beyde Himmel haben /
hier einen und dort wieder einen / der uns anders
lehret / will uns verführen ; An statt / daß wir alle
Dinge solten nach Gottes Wort erforschen / und
die Geister prüfen / ob sie aus Gott seyn / fallen wir
zu schänden und schmähen / das ist ein Schwenck-
felder / Weigelianer / Quacker / Sorimaner und der-
gleichen Ketzer / denen muß man nicht glauben / die
wissen selbst nicht / was sie schreiben oder reden / wo
solten die einfältigen Leute die Klugheit herbekom-
men / sie haben ja nicht studiret / das ist unmöglich /
Gottes Geist kan bey ihnen nicht seyn / ja es sind ein
Theil so gottloß / daß sie solche Dinge dem Teuffel
zuschreiben / und also zu verstehen geben / was sie für

the same way. For GOD cannot watch wickedness any longer. If we do not live better, but rather much worse and more evil than Jews, Turks, and heathens, what use then does GOD have for us? Why do the trees hinder the garden for long if they bring no fruit? They must be cut down and thrown into the fire. Only consider, my dear Christian: is not GOD's Most Holy Name so shamefully misused by us, in that we indeed go to church and listen to GOD's word outwardly, but in fact, and in our hearts, deny its power? Where is true faith, true love, true hope, true patience, true humility? No one trusts the other, no one helps the other, each one is greedy for himself. Where does one speak of GOD's word, where does one act accordingly? Indeed, our life does not agree with the teaching at all. Look only at all estates from the highest to the lowest, what godless behavior goes on therein. No one wants to be persuaded and change their mind. Where is there talk of GOD's word at gatherings, or of true Christendom, where one could build each other up? Only with useless chatter, foolishness, and trifles the noble time is passed and so miserably invested. How many good hours are spent quite uselessly, in drinking, gambling, and other vices; but for a single hour for GOD's praise and honor, we can hardly spare any time, even though we should strive most of all for where we must stay the longest, and for all

sample.seedTranslation: that! Was not Cornelius a heathen? Nevertheless, when he fasted and called upon God, God heard him and helped him onto the right path. How much more we Christians, who are baptized into God's most holy name and can surely take comfort and assurance in our baptismal covenant with God. Why do we not strive for it? Whose is the fault? Is it not ours? Why are we so lazy and negligent regarding the eternal, which lasts into all eternity? It is therefore not God's fault, but our own malice, that we will not obey His voice. We spend most of our life with temporal, perishable existence, which in a moment passes away and we with it, God knows how. Even if Weigelius and other such authors use the same kinds of idioms in their writings, what can we and another upright Christian do about that? All sects and heresies make use of the Holy Scripture; should we for that reason also despise, reject, revile, and slander it? Far be it! They may answer for their own affairs, for what they have written. Each one must give an account for himself and be certain of his own actions, teaching, and life, as he would stand before God on that day. We have the Holy Scripture, Moses and the prophets, the Holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ; that is prescribed to us as a rule and guideline for how we should conduct our life. If we do this, then we act as pious children,

sample.blockSeed: life is a pure cross and tribulation, and thus they live holy and are joyful when they are dissolved from this temporal miserable life. So their dying is only a passage from death into life, for they are still united with Christ in their temporal life and thus remain eternally planted in Him, of which union no person can speak except he who has felt it, for it is the new name that no one knows except he who receives it. Even if they make a misstep and stumble often—as the devil is a crafty spirit who can insinuate himself into all <term>complexions</term> <gloss>constitutions/temperaments</gloss>, thus often tripping them up so that they fall—yet it is God's grace that raises them up again. As soon as the malice has been worked, grace enters their conscience: What have you done? There begins again the sighing and complaining, for God's power is mighty in the weak. The tears do not remain absent until they come to grace again, grow, and thus go in cross and tribulation on the narrow way of eternal life, and are fruitful branches on the vine of Jesus Christ, planted in His garden. They bear heartfelt fruits in deed and truth, do not know themselves, but always think they are still great sinners, inasmuch as their sins and human failings constantly hover before their eyes, as the Holy David laments, yet they always seek to do good until God redeems them from this miserable life, for which they sigh and carry longing hourly and momentarily.

<header>Concluding Speech.</header>
<sig>B iij</sig>

This Judge will not look upon a <term>Primarium</term> <gloss>senior church official</gloss> or his entourage, which he draws to himself, nor any king, prince, or lord of the world according to their possessed power, nor their laws, but will judge the life and test it in His fire. Where will your desecrations and revilements, which you have driven against Christ in His members, remain then? It is written: whoever blasphemes the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness eternally. What, then, do you want to answer for having consciously blasphemed His gift and so wretchedly persecuted the children of Christ? When Christ says, "Whatever you did to these least of my brothers, you did to me," what answer will you then give?

You also despise that I am a layman and have not come from the university with my knowledge, and you spit upon my gift, which I have nevertheless received from GOD as a noble present, which is dearer to me than the whole world. You also desecrate my trade with your spitting and call it, together with my gift, a stench.

How might it go for you when such blasphemies awaken within you in body and soul, and your "fie," with which you spit upon the gift of the Holy Spirit, awakens in you and is ignited by GOD’s wrath, so that the world becomes too narrow for you? What would you then want to give that you had not done such a thing?

Zum 3. lehret es gar ernste Buß-Gebete / wie sich die arme Seele in grossem Ernste / in Christi Verdienst / Leiden Todt und Aufferstehung / ein-wenden / und des bösen irdischen Willens in Chri-sti Todt täglich absterben / wie sie müsse durch Christi Wunden / und Blutvergiessen zum Vat-ter gehen.

Weiln aber der Pasquill saget: Es wären so viel Gotteslästerungen als Zeilen in diesem Büch-lein sind / so ist offenbar / daß er den Geist Christi lästert und schmähet. The <term>Pasquill</term> <gloss>libelous pamphlet</gloss> begins and speaks:
New ways of speaking bring with them common new errors.

->Response.<-

Scripture says: test everything; hold fast to what is good.

->Pasquil.<-

As many lines as there are, so many blasphemies are to be found in the shoemaker’s books, which smell horribly of the shoemaker’s pitch and blacking. Fie, fie, may this stench be far from us.

->Response.<-

The little book teaches the way to Christ very earnestly, how a person should depart from the godless way of this world, enter into true and genuine repentance, and put on Christ in faith. It teaches how one must be born anew in the Spirit of Christ, how one must be renewed in mind and spirit, and how one must follow Christ.

Furthermore, it teaches about true <term>Gelassenheit</term> <gloss>resignation/surrender to God</gloss>, how the penitent person must surrender themselves entirely to GOD, and in Divine trust, begin and complete all their works. It also points out how the devil lays traps and snares for the children of Christ at every hour, and how a person could otherwise not pass through such traps.

sample.seedTranslation:
<header>Defense Speech. Response.</header>

101. O Mr. Primarius! Where does this stand in my book, that I teach men external ecstasy? Show me that, or it will not be so. I teach them the anointing of JESUS CHRIST, with His tender humanity, of a spiritual nature in us, according to the inward ground of faith, of which Christ says: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him; and he who does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man has no life in him <note>John 6:53-56</note>.

102. For that is the temple of the Holy Spirit, as St. Paul says, where Christ’s flesh and blood remain in us. Item: It is the new rebirth, in which the Holy Spirit researches the depth of the Godhead. It is the poured-out Word of the poured-out divine love, which weds and falls in love with our souls, as the entire New Testament teaches, as it is written, etc.

103. Test whether Christ has taken a form in you. If Christ is to gain a form in us, then that must not be absent. If we are to be branches on the vine of Christ, then we must not cling to another: for no one can serve two hearts, says Christ. Item: My Father will give the Holy Spirit to all who ask Him for it. Item: When that same one shall come, he will glorify you.

124. Which makes Satan anxious, that one no longer wants to tolerate him under Christ’s purple mantle. But the time is born that his kingdom is manifest and becomes a mockery; no Primarius will stop that, it is so ordained by GOTT.

->Pasquil.<-

125. Christ has dealt with important things; the cobbler, however, with frivolous things.

->Responsio.<-

126. Christ has brought and shown us the way to salvation, and the cobbler desires to walk upon it; but Satan calls it a frivolous way because it is a cross-way, where a person must in this world, in misery and humility, follow Christ. For Satan is a spirit of pride; therefore you despise the pilgrim-path of Christ, because this path is narrow and straight, and it does not please the fat belly, nor the eyes full of self-honor and selfishness.

127. Christ has destroyed Satan’s kingdom and brought forth Christendom; but the Antichrist has seated himself in Christ’s chair. The cobbler reveals this, through the will of GOD; and that seems to Mr. Primarius to be a frivolous thing, but when the clock strikes seven, it will have been a good thing.

# An den Leser.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Decorative initial L</image-desc>Leber Leser/ ich achte den Pasquill, wohl keiner Antwort werth / weil nur eitel Unwarheit und Lästerung darinnen befunden werden/ ich habe aber um derer Willen eine Antwort machen wollen/ welche es nicht verstehen und mein Büchlein nicht gelesen haben / noch meine Person kennen / welche allein auf das Ansehen des Prim. sehen/ und meynen er lästere mich auß Christlichen Eyffer / und thue solches um Gottes wegen seines Ambts/ wie dan der meinfte Hauffe also irre geführet wird/ daß sie ihm Beyfall geben/ und dencken er thue recht/ es sey den alles wahr/ was er auff der Cankel ausschreiet/ weil er GOttes Namen darin führet/ und mit vermän delt / daß man sein grimmig Herk nicht sehen kan/ sich auch auff sein Ambt beruffet / so glaubet es die Einfalt / welche nichts vom Handel weiß / wie boßhafftiger mich verfolget/ und gank wider sein Ampt handelt / mich auch niemalen darinnen wollen hören. Und richtet das jenige/ das er selber nicht verstehet; so habe ich eine Antwort gemacht / ob mancher wolte sehend werden / und von Lästern wider Gottes Gabe ausgehen/ und bezeige hiemit vor GOtt/ daß ich auß keiner andern Meinung habe geantwortet/ als nur bloß um der Liebe des Nechsten willen / und vermahne den Herrn Primarium sich eines bessern zu besinnen : Dann er hat keinen Löwen/ sondern ein Schäfflein Christi für sich / oder er wird sehen/ in welchen er geflochen hat / daß ihme nicht das Schaff im Geist Christi zum Löwen werde / und das Schaff den Wolff richte / und meyne es herklich und treulich.

blasphemous mouth, and find out, you miserable man, what kind of misfortune is prepared for you.

176. Lord Primarius, keep this traveling money for yourself, for your ascension; I desire nothing from you. Your frivolous insult will surely follow you as traveling money. Do not let yourself long for it: Let him who stands see that he does not fall. Even if you pursue me and intend to banish me, who knows who will also pursue you in a short time.

177. The <term>signatura</term> <gloss>signature/mark</gloss> is already present; it is fitting that you do unto others first, as might happen to you afterward. You must finish filling your measure, and if you do not do penance, the evil spirits might well one day sing such a funeral song for you as well, and tell you to go far away from the countenance of God, for what you do to me now, you do to Christ in his members; He will do the same to you if you do not turn back and do penance.

### Pasquil.

178. You are like Oedipus (he means the Sphinx) whom the earth has swallowed up; oh, guard yourself that something similar does not befall you. This shadow has harmed the people who stood by him very much. But believe me, your shadow harms many of them severely.

fürnehme Leute/ und zwar öffter / und gar in gehei-
mer traulicher Freundschafft / mit ihme umge-
gangen: Also hat ihn sonderlich der Edle Herz von
Franckenberg wol gekennet/und sein Büchlein von
der Buß/Gelassenheit/und dem übersinnlichen Le-
ben Anno 1622. (unter dem Titul / der Weg zu
Christo) allhier zu Görlitz zum Druck befördert/
von diesem von Franckenberg / als um welchen ich
lange Zeit an unterschiedenen Orten/gewesen; auch
abwesende / um seiner erbaulichen conversation
mich nicht zugeben/ per literas vielfältig mit ihme
correspondiret / könte ich viel Zeugnuß beybrin-
gen/daß es J.B.selbst / und nicht ein ander unter sei-
nem Namen/gewesen / bey welchem die Wunder
Gottes offenbar worden: Denn er sie an seiner (des
J.B.) Person nugsam wahr genommen. Ich ge-
schweige derjenigen / so mir auch nicht unbekandt
gewesen / welche durch dieses Mannes Beywoh-
nung und durchdringende Geistes-Rede / in merck-
würdige geschwinde Veränderung ihres Gemü-
thes / und Erneurung ihres Lebens gerathen: Also
da sie zu vorher der Eitelkeit dieser Welt / und den
Lüsten des Fleisches ganz ergeben waren/und gegen
ihre Unterthanen nichts anders als reissende Wöl-
fe sich erzeigten / mit jedermanns Verwunderung
hernach/aller Uppigkeit feind worden / und als ge-
dultige Schaffe mit denselben umgegangen / und
ihr voriges ärgerliches Leben mit steter Reue be-
weinet. Von keinen deren/so ihn erkennet/habe ich
jemaln vernommen / noch durch andere vernehmen
können/

sample.seedTranslation:
Sancyranus lived for no more than five years after Jansenius. An arrogant man, raising himself above all theologians, he so despised the Council of Trent as the work of scholastics and a single Pontiff. What he thought about the doctrine of grace he revealed, being heard to say at one time: "Calvin understood well, but spoke badly." Moreover, being as cautious as possible, he demanded Pythagorean silence from those to whom he spoke ("in secret because of the fear of the Jews," he would say), and he wanted all his letters to be burned. Once, he had imprudently offered poison to a certain priest; he repented immediately, and while the man was proceeding to Poitiers, fearing a denunciation to the local Bishop, he catches up to the man in the middle of his journey and asks to be heard in confession. He then used to tell with a laugh how cunningly he had imposed silence upon a man of dubious faith. A deed worthy of a severe exactor of austere penance! Led by his spirit, the Virgins of Port-Royal deprived themselves of the heavenly bread for many months, even at Easter. The men gave clearer specimens of this penance, some of whom were directors of the Virgins, ascetics, or others who, as penitents, had built their own little huts within the walls of the monastery. For they, not for months but for seven years and more, indeed until the end of their lives, abstained from the table of the Lord as a punishment for their sins.

His first fruit was the *Quaestio Regia* <gloss>Royal Question</gloss>; To what extent is a subject, especially in times of peace, obliged to preserve the life of a prince at the expense of his own life? In it, he reviews more than 30 cases in which he contends that suicide is lawful.

Sacerdoti cuidam minus prudens aliquando venenum propinaverat: statim poenituit, & dum ille Pictavium pergit, delationem ad loci Episcopum veritus, hominem medio in itinere affequitur, seque pro confessione audiri petit: ridens deinde narrare solitus, quam callide viro dubiae fidei silentium imposuisset. Facinus dignum severo austerae poenitentiae exactore! cujus spiritu ductae Virgines Portus Regii per plures menses etiam in Paschate caelesti pane se privarunt. Hi quippe jam non per menses, sed annos septem & ultra, quin ad finem vitae usque in poenam peccatorum suorum a mensa Domini se abstinuerunt.

There, his authority—with the help especially of the two Arnauld sisters, one of whom was the abbess of the nunnery—prevailed to such an extent that, once the previous directors were dismissed, the virgins committed themselves entirely to him, accustomed to think, speak, and act nothing but according to his institute, inflexible against all the exhortations of their superiors, until the community was dissolved and they were dispersed among various houses.

Yet Jansenius himself was not lacking. He would frequently run into France to confer with Sancyranus and his friends. Rassilius of Tours, who was present at such a meeting held in Bordeaux, asserted to two Fathers from the Carmelite Order, Marco Genêt and Nicolas of the Visitation, that the subject of the consultation then was how the authority of the Clergy could be exalted over the monks. Bérulle, who was present, wanted the Clergy to be gathered into communities following his own example; another objected that it would be easier to inspire contempt for the monks in the people than to induce the Clergy to a similar norm of living; others brought forward other means of agitating all Religious. But something else pleased Jansenius for his own cause. A sagacious man, he believed that the whole could be accomplished far more certainly through mutual discord and hatred among the Regulars; wherefore the altercations concerning the *Auxilia* <gloss>a theological dispute regarding divine grace and free will</gloss>, which were then making a great noise, were to be fostered, and the Jesuits were to be made to collide with the other monks so that they might consume each other. And Rassilius confirmed this in writing, supported by his own hand and seal, in the year 1652.

Thus Pascal, I say, not less learnedly and theologically, if you please; unless you prefer to say ironically, by which he mocked his own associates, who did not cease to declaim and write against the Bulls of Innocent and Alexander and other decrees about various nullities. For this writer seemed too fickle to the Jansenists themselves, nay even sometimes of doubtful faith, certainly never fearing to contradict himself if it pleased him, of which he also gave a specimen in the *Provincial Letters*, where he ridicules the doctrine of the Thomist school, which at the beginning he mocks, [but] afterwards commends as his own.

But neither could the power of the King do anything at that time against these men; although he ordered the mandate of accepting the Bull and the same subscription to be entered into the records of the Parliament; and this was an act entirely new and the first of all, by which such a declaration of the King was sent to the Parliament, by which the Pontifical Bull was commanded to be received by royal power as a dogma. The King, therefore, in order to cut off all excuses by which they might exempt themselves from the formula of subscription, requested that a formula be prescribed by the Pontiff himself; that which the Clergy also at the same time begged with highest prayers.

It was done as was requested, and Alexander sent the Bull *Regiminis Apostolici* <gloss>Of the Apostolic Government</gloss> in the year 1664, in which he proposed the following formula to be subscribed by all ecclesiastical men of both Clergy, Bishops, and Archbishops. Porro Dominus Pascal famosus ille auctor litterarum provincialium, quas sub directione Arnaldi conscripserat, has ambages averfatus, nodum expeditius solvit, Bullamque Alexandri pluribus titulis sub- & obreptitiam, atque nullius auctoritatis esse contendit: primo enim ait, omnis solæcismus evertit quamlibet Bullam: & in ipso scripto originali legitur imprimantur pro imprimatur. Deinde omnia præcipiuntur sub pœnis ipso facto incurrendis: sed Papæ non est Regis Franciæ subditis intentare pœnas. Tertio cum Papa dicat: Nos, qui omnia, quæ in hac re gesta sunt, sufficienter & attente perspeximus, utpote qui ejusdem Innocentii jussu, dum adhuc in minoribus constituti Cardinalis munere fungeremur, omnibus illis congressibus interfuimus, quibus apostolicæ auctoritate eadem causa discussa est ea profecto diligentia, qua major desiderari non posset. — — Vult nihil amplius præter Innocentii & suam decisionem requiri: cum tamen dogmata nonnisi Conciliorum auctoritate definita in Ecclesia Gallicana recipiantur. Adhæc nimis abjecte, viliterque loquitur de Ordine Episcopali; cum Chisius, modo Papa, de se jam tum Cardinali Episcopo ait, se in minoribus fuisse. Sed demum hæc absint: cum Papa omnia motu proprio, ex debito Pastoralis Officii, hoc est, ut commentatur, absque Cardinalium consilio & suffragio declaravit, Bullæ auctoritas, & vis omnis per se ruit.

Hoc patrocinio illi quatuor audaciores facti, novis encyclicis ad omnes Episcopos missis, ad rejiciendam omnino Bullam pontificiam eos hortari non dubitarunt. ## Progreſſus Phantaſmatis Janſeniani.

### §. I.
### Initia Queſnelli.

Hae pace Eccleſiæ quies minime reddita fuit, quin turbæ potius auctæ ſunt. Novus enim ſurrexit heros Arnaldo ſuo tempore ſuccenturiandus, Paſcafius Queſnellus Pariſiis natus 1634. & poſtea in Oratorium Berullianum admiſſus. Primum ejus opuſculum: *Quatuor Evangelia cum breviſſimis notis* nonniſi poſt factas plurimis in locis correctiones a Vialardo Cabilonenſi Epiſcopo approbatum an. 1672 prodiit. Minus feliciter alterum emerſit: *Opera S. Leonis magni cum diſſertationibus, notis &c.* Romæ prohibitum altero ab editione anno 1676. ſatis quippe oſtendit, quo ſpiritu ageretur, in Romanæ Sedis auctoritatem iniquiſſimus. Larvam denique penitus poſuit, cum Patres Oratorii an. 1678. ut peſtem janſenianam in viſcera jam admiſſam expellerent, comitia generalia celebrarunt, in iisque doctrinam Janſenii damnatam ſcholis ſuis, & collegiis omnibus proſcripſerunt, formula cunctis ad ſubſcribendum propoſita; Queſnellus enim nec monitis Superiorum, nec minis flexus, pervicaciter continuo reſtitit, & contemptis Regis, & Archiepiſcopi mandatis Pariſiis excedens in latibula ſe abdidit, donec Lutetias ſubinde redux in Belgium evaſit.

maximum, and most efficacious: and grace is always lacking to them throughout their entire life, by which they might be able to fulfill even one single precept without sin.

2nd: "In the state of fallen nature, grace is never restored internally; because the will of man acts merely passively with respect to efficacious grace, and like an inanimate object, it does nothing: it neither cooperates, nor does it consent freely."

3rd: "To merit or demerit in the state of fallen nature, there is no requirement in man for a liberty exempt from natural necessity, even that which is found in indeliberate motions: but it suffices that he be free from coercion."

4th: "The prevenient grace of Jesus Christ is such that the free will of man, moved and excited by it, cannot resist, even if it wished. To assert otherwise is to speak with the <term>Semipelagians</term> <gloss>those who believe human will initiates the movement toward faith</gloss>."

5th: "Jesus Christ died only for the predestined, in such a way that no one except them alone receives true faith and justification through the merits of Christ's death."

These men said that they condemned this sense from the heart, but that they could not subscribe to the formula; since they claimed this was not the sense of <term>Jansenius</term> <gloss>Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres</gloss>. But <term>Jurieu</term> <gloss>Pierre Jurieu, a French Protestant theologian</gloss>, most famous among the <term>Calvinists</term> <gloss>followers of John Calvin</gloss>, chastised these triflers and convinced them that it would be more easily found in the plain and true sense within the books of the Calvinist doctors.

Probavit hanc versionem gallicam Pontanus Doctor Lovaniensis, & Apostolicus librorum Censor, nec obscurus fautor Jansenianorum, eamque utut linguæ tam græcæ, quam gallicæ parum peritus ceu fidelissimam summopere commendavit, adeo, ut Cameracensis, & Namurcensis Episcopi, testimonio censoris confisi suam quoque approbationem, sine ulteriore examine appofuerint. Cum porro etiam Parisiis editio hæc Montensis ab Archiepiscopo prohibita fuit, & ejus exemplaria mandato regii Senatus bibliopolis erepta, non continuerunt se a novis querelis, & clamoribus nascenti operi forte jamjam timentes, & Arnaldus præcipue in delatores, quos credebat, & auctores damnationis, & prohibitionis debacchatus est tanta ferocia, & acerbitate, quæ vel suos offendit, apud quos vix tum mitius, quam alios ob maledicentiam vapulare cœpit. ## Progress of the Jansenist Phantasm.

### §. I.
### The Beginnings of Quesnel.

By this peace, rest was by no means restored to the Church; rather, the disturbances were increased. For a new hero arose, destined to serve as a successor to his <term>Arnauld</term> <gloss>Antoine Arnauld</gloss> in his own time: <term>Pasquier Quesnel</term> <gloss>Jansenist theologian</gloss>, born in Paris in 1634 and later admitted into the <term>Oratory of Bérulle</term> <gloss>The French Oratory, a religious congregation</gloss>. His first little work, "Four Gospels with very brief notes," appeared in 1672 only after corrections had been made in many places, approved by <term>Vialart</term> <gloss>Bishop of Châlons</gloss>, the Bishop of Châlons. The other emerged less happily: "Works of St. Leo the Great with dissertations, notes, etc.," prohibited at Rome in 1676, the year after its edition; indeed, it sufficiently showed in what spirit he was acting, most hostile to the authority of the Roman See. Finally, he threw off the mask completely when the Fathers of the Oratory, in 1678, in order to expel the <term>Jansenist</term> <gloss>Jansenist</gloss> plague already admitted into their vitals, held a general assembly, and in it proscribed the condemned doctrine of <term>Jansenius</term> <gloss>Cornelius Jansen</gloss> from their schools and all their colleges, with a formula proposed to all for subscription; for <term>Quesnel</term>, neither moved by the warnings of his Superiors nor by threats, stubbornly resisted continuously, and, scorning the mandates of the King and the Archbishop, left Paris and hid himself in shelters, until, having returned to Paris from time to time, he escaped to Belgium.

### §. I.
### Initia Queſnelli.

Hae pace Eccleſiæ quies minime reddita fuit, quin turbæ potius auctæ ſunt. Novus enim ſurrexit heros Arnaldo ſuo tempore ſuccenturiandus, Paſcafius Queſnellus Pariſiis natus 1634. & poſtea in Oratorium Berullianum admiſſus. Primum ejus opuſculum: *Quatuor Evangelia cum breviſſimis notis* nonniſi poſt factas plurimis in locis correctiones a Vialardo Cabilonenſi Epiſcopo approbatum an. 1672 prodiit. Minus feliciter alterum emerſit: *Opera S. Leonis magni cum diſſertationibus, notis &c.* Romæ prohibitum altero ab editione anno 1676. ſatis quippe oſtendit, quo ſpiritu ageretur, in Romanæ Sedis auctoritatem iniquiſſimus. Larvam denique penitus poſuit, cum Patres Oratorii an. 1678. ut peſtem janſenianam in viſcera jam admiſſam expellerent, comitia generalia celebrarunt, in iisque doctrinam Janſenii damnatam ſcholis ſuis, & collegiis omnibus proſcripſerunt, formula cunctis ad ſubſcribendum propoſita; Queſnellus enim nec monitis Superiorum, nec minis flexus, pervicaciter continuo reſtitit, & contemptis Regis, & Archiepiſcopi mandatis Pariſiis excedens in latibula ſe abdidit, donec Lutetias ſubinde redux in Belgium evaſit.

Quesnel also praised Gerberon, criticizing nothing in his letters to Boileau, a friend of the Prelate, except that the book was published too quickly and at an inopportune time, namely, when Noailles was called to the Purple <note>the rank of Cardinal</note> by Innocent XII at the request of the King.

Shortly after the *Problem* followed the *Case of Conscience*. The question was asked: whether a confessor has well absolved a cleric who confesses that he does not submit in his mind to the judgment of the Church concerning the text of the Authors, yet displays external submission and reverence to it in silence? The response, subscribed by 40 Theologian Doctors, [was] that this opinion of the Cleric is neither new, nor singular, nor condemned by the Church: [and] that such a person is neither to be urged further, nor held to be suspect. Cardinal Noailles condemned this response as well, and at the same time took care that nothing sinister or injurious be published against the subscribed Doctors, who also all later, except for two, excused the deed.

Meanwhile, when the Quesnellians were planning a new edition of the work, and perceived properly that the condemnation could not be averted by a softer censure, thinking they had to consult for themselves otherwise, they offer it to be examined equally by the celebrated Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux. Then, Abbot Saint-Aignan, when he had sought letters of confirmation from Rome for his Bishopric, lest he succumb to the envy and deceitful arts of the Jansenists even in Rome, as the worst advisors were suggesting, allowed himself to be persuaded to defend the fourth proposition of Jansen in the Sorbonne itself.

But these threats soon vanished. Since neither the acts of the Parliament nor the error of the abbot seemed of such importance that they could stir a prudent suspicion that acceptance would be denied, and the Dauphin had even given in writing a public testimony of the Catholic faith and his firm adherence to it, after two years of exhaustion finally spent on examinations and the collation of texts, the famous Bull *Unigenitus* <gloss>Only-Begotten</gloss> was signed by Clement XI on September 8, 1713, after everything had first been examined and the points revised by Trémoille, and it was published two days later, on September 10. In it, one hundred and one propositions excerpted from the work of Quesnel are condemned "in the lump," as they say, namely, as false, impious, heretical, etc., with these and other censures added to be applied respectively to each. It is added that many other similar and related propositions are contained therein that are worthy of condemnation, and that the text of the scripture itself is corrupted by the disapproved Montenfus edition. Wherefore the whole book, published or to be published in any language, is prohibited and condemned.

The Pope replied that he would be content if the Opponents accepted the Bull in relation to the instruction of those 40 Bishops; but it was not this, but another, namely with various restrictions and distinctions of senses, that Cavalier demanded. § 4.
*Appeal to a General Council.*

The thunders of the Vatican were now being prepared; Noailles was judged by the College of Cardinals itself to be unworthy of the purple. Nevertheless, time was still given to repent, from the hope that the Opponents had shown by having completed a certain scheme of doctrine, which, when it was not approved by those accepting, they offered them a writing of three columns, similar to that Jansenist one of old, in the middle column of which were the propositions of Quesnell themselves, on one side the obvious sense, on the other some other Catholic one, or at least one capable of excuse.

The arrival of Cavalier was little accepted at Rome, also because he had brought with him P. Laborde from the Oratory, a well-known supporter of Quesnell. Soon after the second day of his arrival, Clement XI summoned all the Cardinals early in the morning. In a brilliant speech, he exposed the deplorable state of the Gallican Church, the obstinacy of many, and the frauds of some of the Bishops themselves, and while he argued the cause of the Bull with most weighty words, having finally fallen into the point that those opposing the acceptance of the Bull were accustomed to use for their defense—namely, that the liberty of the Gallican Church would be overturned by this very obstinacy of theirs—he demonstrated it invincibly. "This," he said, "turns on two main heads as if on as many hinges: first, that it is for the Bishops to judge on a matter of faith in the first instance; second, that they hold as legitimate that they can even interpret the Bulls of the Pontiffs." Indeed, the first had been done, and without his opposition, in that numerous Convent of the Clergy and Bishops held in the year 1714; the second had been performed no less completely by them through the instruction added to the acceptance, which was likewise approved by him. If these things did not suffice, there would be no authority of the Episcopal Order henceforth, no legitimate power of judging or interpreting, that is, one easily eluded by anyone, and there would be no Bull, no law of the Church, which they would be bound to accept if they did not wish to. And with these, all the Duke’s plans conceived in his mind for bringing the Cardinal back to the path were finally overturned.

Meanwhile the Appellants triumphed, though not without grief for the death of Quesnel, their leader most esteemed after Arnauld, from whom all this present cause was derived. It is not pleasing here to weave the history of this man’s life; it is helpful to add only two things worthy of memory to what has already been said about him. The first is a certain writing sent by Quesnel himself to a certain Priest, who, having at last wiped away the darkness of errors, was returned to himself and the Church, and produced it. These were rules comprised in 12 articles, which his own were to use in conversation among themselves and with various kinds of men. The sum was almost this: Union and concord: faith in the secret: circumspection in speech according to the varying condition of men: ambiguity <note>original: "amphibologia"</note> in various heads of Religion: he wished it to be said that they use Christ present in the Eucharist, not only by faith or figure, as the heterodox do, but neither by transubstantiation or substantially or really, as Catholics say: how then? in an imperceptible manner. In the Sacrament of penance, they were to urge the insufficiency of attrition and the necessity of perfect contrition. That they should openly impugn sufficient grace, the liberty of indifference, and merits, and at other times through the vagueness of words, so that a way out might be open to the pressed: that they should uniquely extol victorious grace: and thus many other things. sample.blockSeed: the Cardinal criticized the obscurity of the Bull and appealed only conditionally, should the explanation be denied; they, however, absolutely accused and rejected the Bull as contrary to Catholic dogma and to the Decalogue itself. Nor was there delay; by order of the Duke, this writing was condemned and suppressed by the Parliament as having been published against the law of silence. Noailles indeed protested that the publication of his appeal had been done without his knowledge, yet he rejoiced to see it received by almost his entire diocese; indeed, having become bolder, when the Pope initially dissembled everything, awaiting the formula of acceptance to be sent by the Cardinal, he dared to demand not only an explanation of the Bull conformable to the submitted scheme of doctrine, but besides this, also a Brief to all the faithful, by which the Constitution *Unigenitus* would be derogated: nor was this enough; instead of the formula of acceptance, he finally sends an *apostilla* <note>original: "apostillam"</note> <gloss>marginal note/appendix</gloss> to Rome, by which he declares that he neither seeks an explanation nor a Brief, nor cares for it, unless in addition silence were imposed on everyone concerning the question of fact. Then indeed the Pontiff, moved by this insolent temerity and obstinacy, when he had simultaneously understood that the scheme of doctrine proposed by the acceptors had been changed in 25 articles and 48 propositions, the beginning and end altered, mutilated, and full of deceitful substitutions of phrases (as, when it was being read, "the Bull condemns, the Pope condemns," it was replaced by the opponents with "the Bull wishes to condemn, the intention of the Pope was to condemn"), had been offered to him, he orders that instrument of appeal to be condemned by the Holy Office <note>original: "S. Officio"</note>, and the decree was posted in the Campo dei Fiori on February 8, 1718, nor did he permit the apostolic letters of confirmation to be dispatched for the three nominated by the King for the mitres,

sample.seedTranslation:
The Cardinal, before he would accept the bull, requested that it be examined. Upon these being rejected, he proposed a formula to be signed, by which he would not only accept the bull simply, but also retract all that he had written wrongly in his pastoral Instruction. At the same time, having convened a particular council in the Lateran Basilica, he declared the constitution *Unigenitus* <note>original: "Unigenitus" - a papal bull issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713, condemning the errors of Pasquier Quesnel</note> as a Rule of faith. Since Noailles was still prevaricating, he broke off all further communication with him. King Louis XV also suppressed by decree those same twelve articles which shameless peddlers of nonsense had published as if submitted by the Pope himself for the explanation of the bull.

Driven so often and so strongly, the Cardinal finally seemed to waver; he was certainly deliberating about promulgating the Bull. The letter of his thirty parish priests caused a delay, who, after it had been suppressed and torn up by the King's order, openly declared by means of flying papers and voices that they would be under the authority of one God and an ecumenical council. Added to this were the examples and exhortations of his three principal episcopal colleagues of Sens, Montpellier, and Auxerre, under whose name and approval, and under whose auspices, whole reams of mandates, instructions, letters, professions of faith, notes, and other papers filled with errors and calumnies were produced. Noailles did not, in fact, approve of this much anymore: yet he was held back; he hesitated, although he saw greater scandals and detriments to the Church always growing gradually. For when the Carthusians were holding a general convention in Paris in the year 1725, and there had decreed that the acceptance of the Bull was to be performed by all their members, fifteen of them appealed to the Parliament,

The Cardinal, before he would accept the bull, requested that it be examined. Upon these being rejected, he proposed a formula to be signed, by which he would not only accept the bull simply, but also retract all that he had written wrongly in his pastoral Instruction. At the same time, having convened a particular council in the Lateran Basilica, he declared the constitution *Unigenitus* <note>original: "Unigenitus" - a papal bull issued by Pope Clement XI in 1713, condemning the errors of Pasquier Quesnel</note> as a Rule of faith. Since Noailles was still prevaricating, he broke off all further communication with him. King Louis XV also suppressed by decree those same twelve articles which shameless peddlers of nonsense had published as if submitted by the Pope himself for the explanation of the bull.

Driven so often and so strongly, the Cardinal finally seemed to waver; he was certainly deliberating about promulgating the Bull. The letter of his thirty parish priests caused a delay, who, after it had been suppressed and torn up by the King's order, openly declared by means of flying papers and voices that they would be under the authority of one God and an ecumenical council. Added to this were the examples and exhortations of his three principal episcopal colleagues of Sens, Montpellier, and Auxerre, under whose name and approval, and under whose auspices, whole reams of mandates, instructions, letters, professions of faith, notes, and other papers filled with errors and calumnies were produced. Noailles did not, in fact, approve of this much anymore: yet he was held back; he hesitated, although he saw greater scandals and detriments to the Church always growing gradually. For when the Carthusians were holding a general convention in Paris in the year 1725, and there had decreed that the acceptance of the Bull was to be performed by all their members, fifteen of them appealed to the Parliament,

<header>TO THE GALLIC CHURCHES.</header>
<sig>A.iij.</sig>

Osiander is rather an enemy of your salvation, while he tries to lead you away from the Gospel and the doctrine that you already have as most certain from the word of God, to another. Furthermore, as to the peace of the Gallic Churches with the German Churches of God, who is a Christian—I do not say so devoid of all Christian mind, but so alien to all humanity—that he would not himself desire it above all things, and beg for it from God the Best and Greatest with every prayer and tear of his heart? To me, certainly, this sentiment of Augustine has always seemed golden: *The good of peace is such that even in earthly and mortal affairs nothing is usually heard that is more pleasing, nothing more desirable to be longed for, nothing finally more excellent to be found.* I would call a beast, and indeed a monstrous one, a most cruel <term>alastora</term> <gloss>avenging spirit/fiend</gloss> of the human race, a public enemy of his own fatherland, a most hostile persecutor of the Church of God, any man, Brothers, who either does not want, or hates, peace to exist between the Churches of God; and especially between the Gallic and German ones, since the origin, the most ancient kinship, and the highest consensus in other matters are the same for those peoples, and their benevolence toward each other has always been the highest, and there are even many benefits of the German race toward our own. These great bonds of friendship themselves exhort both Churches sufficiently to enter into that sweetest peace, or rather to preserve what was long ago entered into and confirmed. Who is this, therefore, who so falsely divines that enmities, hatred, and wars exist or are being prepared between pious Frenchmen and Germans? This, certainly, we have never believed before, as you know, Brothers, nor do we persuade ourselves of it even now. For although there are certain controversies between us on matters not of the least moment, we have decided to treat them with Christian moderation of character, and not on that account to break the peace; and if, because our sins press us so, any agreement on these matters cannot yet exist between us, we have nevertheless learned, and want, and are able to tolerate kindly and fraternally those who disagree with us, according to Paul's precept. For Gregory the Great excellently says, following the same Paul: *Whoever does not care to keep peace refuses to bear the fruit of the spirit. For whoever desires to be an heir of the heavenly Father must guard the peace.* And would that, Osiander, by you we might at last be allowed to see and experience that sweetest and most long-awaited time, in which it can be truly said concerning the Churches of God, as Luke writes in Acts: *The Churches had peace, and were built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the consolation of the Holy Spirit, were multiplied.* For blessed, indeed most blessed, Osiander, are the <term>eirēnopoioi</term> <gloss>peacemakers</gloss>, as our Lord Jesus Christ says. Those are they, however, who are not only themselves ready with the most prepared mind to accept a pious peace (whom Bernard calls "placid"), but also those who, by any means, conciliate and foster the peace and concord of God among others. Everyone knows that you are by no means of the kind or number of those (whatever you may feign or dissimulate here) who have read those virulent earlier *Antisturmian* writings of yours published against us, and your savage condemnations of us. And so, the adornments are for the public; I know you from within and under the skin <note>A classic idiom for knowing someone's true nature.</note>. But you should remember, Dearest ones, what Jerome writes about John, Bishop of Jerusalem (who, while he was in fact sowing most grievous errors in the Church of God, nevertheless offered peace to the Churches with his words): *It is nothing great to profess peace with one's voice and destroy the work of peace; to sound concord with words, and demand servitude in reality. We also want peace, and we not only want it, but we ask for it: but the peace of Christ.*

# AD ECCLES. GALL.

At tūc præfens aderat Moses ipse & vir & maritus Sephorae, nec tantū in eodē erat hospitio, sed in eodem cubiculo, adeò vt Sephora irata præcisum filiorum præputium ad pedes Mosis abiecerit. Deinde Sephora nō alienos, sed suos tantùm circumcidit. Et tamen Osiander hoc mulieribus veluti obstetricib⁹ permittit, (quēadmodum ex eorum vsu & praxi apparet) vt etiam alienos liberos baptizare possint. Quid ergo Sephorae exemplum ad Osiandri sententiam, cum contraria potius ex eo colligantur? Nimirum etsi vir adsit, posse mulierem baptizare non quofuis, sed suos tantùm liberos. Haec igitur est prima ad hoc exemplum Sephorae nostra responsio. Altera verò est, quod tum ex particulari generale quiddam colligit: tum ex facto extraordinario regula perpetua cōstituit, cùm nusquā alibi legamus mulieres in Dei populo, & sub lege suos vel alienos liberos circūcidisse. Praeterea in ipsius adeo Mosis contumeliam ac reprehensionem hoc quoque fuit. Dominus enim ea ratione Mosem nimiae negligentiae per vxorem arguit, quod filios suos nō circumcidisset, & sacrosanctum illud Dei foedus cum sua familia, praetermittens circūcisionem, neglexisset. Denique quis non videt in eo dissimilem fuisse Baptismi & Circumcisionis rationem? Nusquam enim legimus Circumcidi-di munus olim Sacerdotib⁹ peculiariter à Deo mandatum fuisse, quoniam Circumcisio etiam ante segregatos à reliquo populo Sacerdotes, & à Deo instituta, & à populo vsurpata fuerit, annis plusquam quadringētis. <header>AD ECCLES. GALLIC.</header>

To conclude this point, although the works and judgments of God are hidden and unknown to us, they are nevertheless always most just. Nor does it follow that if He is occupied in the same work as we humans, He nonetheless operates viciously, as we do. But because you are very often and very rightly instructed about these matters by your Pastors, and because the scope of this entire disputation is solely to demonstrate that the teaching of this monitor <note>referring to Lucas Osiander</note> is both false and by no means full or sincere, I do not think it necessary to add more on this subject, even though it is a far weightiest argument.

->CONCERNING IDOLS.<-

It remains, therefore, that we also briefly discuss the chapter he added last. It concerns idols. This was not mentioned by Osiander so much out of any necessity of time or of idolatry (which, by the grace of God the Best and Greatest, remains absent among you), but rather to publicly defame all of you, however untimely the occasion he seized upon, and to bring you into hatred and ill will before all Magistrates. For what other purpose does that tail <note>a metaphorical reference to the final section of Osiander’s work</note> of yours have, Osiander, other than for you to vomit forth your poison against us under that honeyed speech and that <term>θεοφρονήσει</term> <gloss>reverent thoughtfulness/divine wisdom</gloss> most exquisitely written by the correction of all your colleagues, and for you to wish for us to be held guilty? Therefore, in that entire writing of yours, the voice indeed was the voice of Jacob, but the hands were the hands of Esau <note>a reference to Genesis 27:22; meaning the words seemed pious, but the intent was hostile</note>, that is, yours. Therefore, you accuse us verbosely because in these civil wars of ours, certain idols were <unclear>in some places by our people</unclear> <column-break/>

<summary>Daneau concludes his discussion on divine providence and transitions to refuting Osiander’s accusations regarding the treatment of idols during civil conflicts.</summary>

distinguished). Finally, the causes of our Predestination should have been explained in this place, not from that Prescience of God, but from the Decree itself and the ordination of his Providence. For the Prescience or Foreknowledge of God, <term>πρόγνωσις</term> <gloss>foreknowledge</gloss> in Greek, is properly the cause of nothing. But <term>ὁρισμὸς</term> <gloss>definition/decree</gloss>, <term>προορισμὸς</term> <gloss>predestination</gloss>, <term>βουλὴ</term> <gloss>counsel</gloss>, <term>πρόνοια</term> <gloss>providence</gloss>, the decree, counsel, and ordination of God, these are the causes of all things. From which it happens that Osiander everywhere calls God "foreknowing" and "foreseeing," but never "ordaining," "decreeing," etc., not even when he deals with Predestination and the eternal salvation of God's elect, where it was most necessary. It is as if God sits in heaven like some idle spectator of events (which happen here by men), while he himself decrees nothing about them. And certainly, this is a fraud and doctrine of those Papists who think most poorly about the reprobation of God, which this benevolent monitor of yours embraces and complains is not delivered to you as to the Gallican Churches which are reformed and truly instructed from the word of God. Therefore, since he demonstrates that he was ignorant of the very sources of the predestination of men in this place, how, I ask you, can he teach correctly anything about it, either to you or to his own? Furthermore, a fourth error of his in this argument is that he interprets these most express words of God speaking about Pharaoh, "I have raised thee," as "I foreknew that you would be impious." And "The Lord hardened Pharaoh," that is, he made him hard by accident, just as the Law is said to generate concupiscences in us; and he who gives good advice to a perverse man who does not obey the advice seems to make him worse. THE LAST NUMBER IS CONCLUDED
Observation XIX follows.

OBSERVATION XIX. ON LOCAL VISITATION.

*On the Visitation of Ecclesiastical Persons.*

Firstly, let every parish priest and beneficiary be interrogated regarding his name, surname, parents, and birthplace. Then, let the letters of investiture and admission to the cure be requested from him, if he holds a beneficed cure.
Thirdly, let him be interrogated how often he confesses in a year and to whom.
Fourthly, let his books be seen: whether, besides others, he has a Breviary of Constance with a Directory, the Roman Catechism, the Council of Trent, and the Synodal Statutes of this Diocese: also a book on cases of conscience, and indeed some approved postils <note>Collections of sermons or commentaries on scriptures</note>, as they are called, with Bibles, and let him read these diligently.
Fifthly, let the Visitors sometimes make an experiment with the simpler and suspicious ones by interrogating them regarding various things pertaining to the canonical hours, the ceremonies of the Church, and the administration of the sacraments, whether they are practiced in them or not.

I acknowledge the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church as the mother and teacher of all churches; and I pledge and swear true obedience to the Roman Pontiff, the successor of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and Vicar of Jesus Christ.

Likewise, I undoubtedly receive and profess all other things handed down, defined, and declared by the sacred Canons and ecumenical Councils, and especially by the most holy Council of Trent. <header>Defense Speech.</header>

He cannot do without the shoemaker, after all, and has a concern that the shoemaker might soil his honor, therefore he merely forbids it. O Lord Primarius, the shoemaker has his title within himself; you cannot soil it; he will keep it eternally.

### Pasquil.

157. Christ gave the thirsty water of life to drink, but the shoemaker runs every morning to the brandy, or water of death.

### Responsio.

158. Christ offers his children the water of eternal life even today, and gives them to drink of his blood of love; he also gives me that same water to drink for my thirsty soul; for that I thank him eternally, that he has made me alive and seeing through this water; I drink that same water, and that is a water for and against death, about which the Lord Primarius speaks in a perverted way.

159. But that he says I run to brandy every morning, that is not at all true; I neither can nor want to drink brandy, and I have had enmity with brandy for a long time, so that I do not even like to smell it; it is repulsive to me; it surprises me that the Lord Primarius, as a high priest, errs so greatly; it becomes him very badly; if a common man did that, one would say: He is a liar. I hardly know what I should give in answer to such an untruth.

hin / O nein! wir Armen haben sie nicht zu bezahlen! wir müssen mit einem Trunck Bier vorlieb nehmen / aber dem Herrn Primarius, muß man wohl ausländische Wein geben / wenn gleich andere Leuthe müssen mit geringern vor lieb nehmen.

164. Die Spanische Wein machen / daß man den Herrn Primarium bisweilen verleurt: Auch siehet mans an der Wein Blüt unter seinem Angesichte / daß er vielmehr starcke Wein trincket als ich / denn ich habe keine solche Zeichen wie er / er trincket in einer Wochen mehr frembden Wein / als ich im ganzen Jahr nicht trincke.

165. Aber ich verstehe fast wol / wo dem Hasen das Bein gebrochen ist / er weiß / daß ich durch Göttliche Schickung bin öffters / zu grossen Herrn und von Adeln bingeführet worden / so dencket er / wan wir zusammen komen / wir sitzen beyeinander und sauffen uns voll / wie er bey seiner Gesellschafft pfleget. Aber nein! die Edeln und Gewaltige / welchen mit voll sauffen dienet ist / die lassen mich nicht zu sich fordern / nur Gottsfürchtige fromme Herzen / denen ihre Seeligkeit Ernst ist.

166. Es ist aber Herr Primarius nur eine Mißgunst: Er gedencket es gehe ihm etwas ab / aber er dörffte das wohl nicht fürchten / diese Leuthe / welcher meiner begehren / die begehren wohl seiner nicht. Es ist ein grosser Unterscheid zwischen Heucheln und die Warheit ins Gesicht sagen / der Herr Primarius glaube es oder nicht / es ist nicht meine Gewohnheit dem Reichen zu Heucheln / um Geschencke und Gaben / wie er meinet.

Er kan doch der Schuster nicht entbehren/ und hat Sorge/ der Schuster möchte ihme Ehr besudeln/ darum verbeut er sie nur. O Herz Primarius, der Schuster hat seinen Titel in sich/ ihr könnet ihn nicht besudeln/ er wird ihme ewig behalten.

### Pasquil.

157. Christus hat den durstigen Wasser des Lebens zu trincken gegeben/ der Schuster aber laufft alle Morgen zum Brandwein/ oder Wasser des Todes.

### Responsio.

158. Christus beut noch heutiges Tags/ seinen Kindern Wasser des ewigen Lebens an/ und träncket sie mit seinem Blute der Liebe/ desselben Wassers gibt er meiner durstigen Seele auch zu trincken/ des dancke ich ihme ewiglich/ daß er mich hat durch dieses Wasser lebendig und sehend gemacht/ dasselbe Wasser trincke ich/ und das ist ein Wasser für und wider den Todt/ wieder Herz Primarius verkehrter Weise davonreder.

159. Daß er aber saget/ ich lauffe alle Morgen zum Brandwein/ das ist gar nicht war/ ich kan noch mag keinen Brandwein trincken/ und habe lange Zeit Feindschafft mit dem Brandwein gehabt/ daß ich ihn auch nicht gerne rieche/ er ist mir zu wider/ es wundert mich/ daß der Herz Primarius, als ein Hoherpriester/ also sehr fehlet/ es stehet ihm doch gar übel an; Wann das ein gemeiner Mann thäte/ so würde man sagen: Er wäre ein Lügner/ ich weiß fast nicht/ was ich soll für solche Unwarheit zur Antwort geben.

But because these are true, you perceive, beloved brothers, how inept Osiander's reasoning is. Another [argument] follows, no less invalid than that one, and yet repeated by him in almost infinite places, both here and in the book against Sturmius.

*There is one merely spiritual manducation of the flesh of Christ, about which John chapter 6 treats; another is sacramental, which is instituted in the Supper of the Lord. Therefore the very flesh of Christ in the sacramental [manducation] is In, Under, and With that Bread, and that Wine in a manner of corporal presence: and is taken together with the sign itself by anyone approaching the Supper, even with an impure mouth.* Answer. As if, although sacramental manducation has signs for the sake of teaching and relieving our infirmity, which a merely spiritual manducation does not have; yet the very thing of the Sacrament, namely the flesh of Christ (which is one and the same in both, that is, in spiritual and in Sacramental manducation) is eaten in a different manner, and with a different mouth, in this sacramental one than in that merely spiritual one. And that manner, or the mouth suitable for eating the flesh of Christ itself, is faith. What then? Osiander is deceived, and indeed childishly, who thinks that the flesh of Christ itself is different, or is eaten differently, in spiritual manducation than in sacramental. But if the flesh of Christ is the same, then it is received with the same mouth, with the same teeth, with the same stomach: namely, spiritually, not corporally: by faith, not by the mouth: by the spirit, not by the belly. <meta>continues from previous page: learned this miserable subterfuge</meta> from the Papists, that the Fathers are not to be compared with us, but only among themselves: as if Paul were saying that all those who were in the desert ate the same spiritual food among themselves, but not the same that we eat; this (I say) is a vain subterfuge, and is refuted by the very words of Paul. For Paul immediately adds that these things were types of our own: and he compares us with the Fathers, not the Fathers among themselves, most openly in that whole passage. Since, therefore, those Fathers ate the flesh of Christ, they must also have had the same present, and yet, since it did not yet exist by the nature of things, it certainly cannot be said to have been present in, under, and with that Manna and that drink in a manner of corporal and real presence. There was, therefore, a sacramental presence, because the Manna and the drink were sacraments to them, just as that Bread and that Wine are to us. There was a <term>schetikē</term> <gloss>relative</gloss> and covenantal presence, just as in a ring that is given by a bridegroom to a bride, the betrothal, the words, and the faith of the bridegroom are present (says Bernard). Therefore, although we deny a corporal presence and the real cohesion of the same, that is, of the essential flesh and blood of Christ with the very signs of the Holy Supper of the Lord, we by no means say for that reason that the Supper is without the blood and flesh of Christ, or that we celebrate it without the thing itself that is signified, provided that one receives those signs and sacraments with faith. But since it is to have refuted the arguments of this man against us, let us briefly see how he overturns our Churches' understanding regarding that true presence of the flesh and blood of Christ in the Supper of the Lord, but <term>schetikē</term> <gloss>relative</gloss> and covenantal. Thus, therefore, he refutes us.

The gifts which Christ received without measure from the Father as he is man do not overturn the nature of his human flesh and its essential properties. For it does not follow that, if the most invincible Emperor, who acts in Austria, has the right of imperial power in Speyer and exercises it, he is also at the same time in Speyer by the Rhine as he is in Vienna by the Danube.

The fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ corporally. Therefore, Christ can place his flesh everywhere. Answer. And these, dearest brothers, are all the minutest arguments of this monitor who is enticing you toward a new doctrine; how inept, absurd, <term>asyllogista</term> <gloss>illogical</gloss>, and even blasphemous they are, you yourselves can easily see, as I hope you already do. For a word is sufficient to the wise, as the old proverb says. Although there were enough ineptitudes and errors in what Osiander has written up to this point, for a conclusion he wanted to add others no less significant, so that, compelled by the force of truth and imprudently, he might reveal to you the foulness, not to say impiety, of that doctrine which he yet exhorts you to embrace. That doctrine which he adds, and which follows entirely from the oral manducation <note>the theory that the body of Christ is eaten physically by the mouth</note>, is that even the unworthy—not the Turks, not the Jews, not the Pagans as he calls them (for they would neither approach the supper nor be admitted if known)—but those who externally profess the name of Christ, yet inside are mockers of God, impious and faithless men approaching the supper, he wants, with his impious and impure mouth, to partake of the most sacred body of Christ itself. What more horrible thing can be said? You, indeed, dearest brothers, have not so learned Christ: but rather that those are the true words of Christ (who is the truth and wisdom of God itself), *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.* Therefore, Augustine, explaining this statement of Christ excellently (to omit Cyril and others), says, *when Christ is eaten, either life itself is eaten, and the thing of the sacrament is for every man unto life, and for no one unto destruction, whoever has been a partaker of it.* Therefore the unworthy, faithless, mockers, and impious, approaching the Lord’s

Quanquam autem in iis, quæ ad hunc vsque locum perscripsit Osiander, satis inerat ineptiarum, & errorum: pro colophone tamen alios quoque non minores addere voluit, vt vobis eius doctrinæ (ad quæ tamē amplectendam vos exhortatur) turpitudinem, ne dicam impietatem, vi veritatis coactus & im prudens reuelaret. Illa autem, quam addit, & quæ omnino ex orali manducatione sequitur, doctrina est, quòd etiam indignos, nō Turcas, non Iudæos, nō Paganos quos vocat, (nec enim illi vel ad cœnam accederent, vel noti admitterentur) sed ipsum Christi nomen externè quidem profitentes, & intus tamen Dei irrisores, impios & infideles homines ad cœnam accedentes vult iste ore suo impio & impuro ipsum sacratissimum Christi corpus manducare. Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, who is God and has no place: yet it does not follow that the flesh of Christ is not in heaven as in a place, since it is one thing for the flesh of Christ to be in heaven, and another to sit at the right hand of the Father; these two things, however, Osiander confuses here, as he does everywhere.

<margin>Pag. 35.</margin> Christ the man has power over all things. Therefore the flesh of Christ is everywhere corporally present. Answer. Now we have endured you, Osiander, as one ignorant of all things for too long. Why, therefore, do you judge the French Churches, and the pious who are in them, to whom you write these things, to be trunks or blocks, that they cannot immediately sniff out these ineptitudes of yours, which reveal themselves plainly to even the blind, not to mention the bleary-eyed and the barbers, by these arguments of yours?

The right hand of God does not signify the circumference or circumscription of a place? Therefore the flesh of Christ (which is at the right hand of God) is not to be established in any place by circumscription of place. Answer. You would truly say this if the flesh of Christ itself were the right hand of God itself! Even if there were a true and legitimate inference from power to the position and "where" of a person. And so you plainly confuse two articles of our faith: he descended into heaven, which shows the place of Christ’s flesh: and he sits at the right hand of the Father, which declares his right and status in the heavens themselves.

<margin>Pag. 36.</margin> Christ fills all things in all. Therefore the flesh is everywhere present. Answer. Not by the presence of his flesh: but by the power of his Spirit, according to the efficacy of his virtue, Christ fills all things, as we have already said.

That place of heaven where the flesh of Christ is cannot be demonstrated by fingers or eyes. Therefore the flesh of Christ is not in heaven. These are the Achillean arguments <note>i.e., his "strongest" arguments</note> of this man.

<summary>Daneau continues to dismantle Osiander’s arguments, highlighting his confusion between Christ’s divinity and humanity and his failure to distinguish between biblical figures of speech and physical location.</summary>

sample.seedTranslation: and those who are ill for a long time also die with tranquility. From that, I elicit that from a tranquil or heavy resolution, the soul cannot be elicited from the body in a good or bad state after this life, as some ignorant people argue, because death follows the disposition of nature by the law of all. But it is by divine dispensation. Sometimes the saints die much more painfully than the reprobate, and sometimes conversely. For we read that Augustine, Martin, and Bernard departed in heavy pains. And we also read of others who died in such tranquility that their bodies could not even be buried, as Gregory narrates of a certain count who was found to be as holy as he had been believed to be, long after he had rested in the tomb, from the fragrance of his body and the integrity of his body. In the Lives of the Fathers, we also read of two married people, a holy man and a vicious wife, whose husband died with great lack of tranquility and pain, but the woman died with great tranquility and peace. And afterward, it was revealed that the husband was blessed, but the wife was damned. For God purges the elect in the present so that they may be secure afterward. Conversely, he remunerates the reprobate here for their good deeds so that they have nothing to hope for regarding their reward in the future, as is evident in Luke 16 concerning the rich glutton and the holy Lazarus. We believe, however, that the blessed mother of the Lord, Mary, migrated from this age without pain, just as she gave birth to the Savior of the ages without pain. And similarly, John, to whom the Virgin was entrusted at the cross. And we find very many elect of God preserved from the pains of death by a special privilege. Therefore, he who hopes to possess a peaceful resolution of his body should study to preserve his life in innocence, for a bad death, even if it is painful, does not follow a good life. But who leads the souls out as they depart from the body, since they are no longer in their own power? It is necessary, therefore, that they be led by others. To this, although we do not find a certain answer in the scriptures, we can estimate that the angels to whom they are committed lead them out, or if they are to be damned, also.

### ¶ Regarding the departure of human souls from bodies by the sentence of death.

**A**s far as the first point is concerned, it must be known that, as is evident from the revelations of some, the separation of the soul from the body is most painful. For that penalty exceeds all the pains of the world, although it is not felt by other men. The reason for this is primarily because the natural appetite of the soul for the body is ruptured, and the violation of this natural appetite is very painful. Just as also in the death of another, namely a wife or children or friends, the grief is heavy. As it is read of Saint Augustine, to whom it seemed that at the death of his dear friend, half of his heart had been taken away. Also, the soul, before its infusion into the body, had no place anywhere, but was created by being infused and infused by being created. Therefore, it is ignorant of where it will be led after death and in what state it is to be placed. It knows, indeed, from scripture that there are many places for souls, but it is ignorant of the place assigned to it. We also read of the souls of the elect that they left their bodies with difficulty, as is evident in the Lives of the Fathers, that angels descended to a certain destitute pilgrim lying in the street, who encouraged his soul to depart, which was trembling to leave, until most sweet melody coming from heaven with sweet modulations released it from the body. Thus we read of many that celestial choirs were heard rejoicing at the death of the saints. But the soul withdraws from the body because of the intemperance of the body, from the discrepancy and distraction of the qualities and humors in the body. Thence, indeed, the vital spirits through which the soul operates in the body grow coarse and fail, and the powers of the soul, both vegetative and sensitive, are rendered incapable of operating as instruments, because the soul can do nothing without them, even in the acts of the intellective power. From the third book On the Soul: It is necessary for every intelligent being to consider phantasms.

tempting him whether it was lawful to give tribute to Caesar or not. "Show me," he said, "the coin of the tribute." And they offered him a denarius having in itself the image of Caesar and the superscription with the determined weight. This pertains to our proposition: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Certainly Caesar's. It is to be observed, therefore, first whether that appearing spirit has the image of Christ, who is the truth, by His own testimony: "I am the way, the truth, and the life." Which truth excludes all falsity, vanity, and lying. If, therefore, it is found in this spirit that it mingles no falsity, vanity of boastful praise, and arrogance in its manifestation, it is to be presumed to be of a good spirit. If, however, in the opposite mode, it is to be held as suspect, just as in the temptation of Christ, Matthew 4: it suggested gluttony, vain glory, and avarice. And in the temptation of the first woman, it suggested the desire of loftiness, saying: "You shall be as God." And it swore, saying: "For God knows." For that spirit is a liar and the father of lies, nor did it stand in the truth, but is deceitful and fraudulent, and such things proceed from its heart even if it speaks the truth, as is evident in the Gospel, where it is ordered by Christ to be silent even about the truth, because it covers its deceitfulness under it.

<margin>Fourth Mode</margin>
The fourth mode of discerning is if there is the superscription on the denarius, that is, apostolic doctrine and a teacher approved by the church, so that nothing be in the responses of that spirit or in its gestures that derogates from the faith, or from good morals and the rites of the church according to canon laws or conciliar decrees, or against the institutions of the Holy Roman Church. And this is against heretics, deceivers, sorcerers, diviners, and enchanters. The vessel of election, Paul, certifies us to the Galatians 1: "But though we or an angel from heaven preach a gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema." is it. However, nothing superfluous, curious, useless, or superstitious is to be investigated from it, unless it wishes to reveal those things of its own accord. In festive days and at a sober time, namely before the midday meal, I think it is more convenient for this inquiry to be made, or perhaps if it pleases God at the time of night, as is accustomed to be done. But if by chance no sign appears at that hour, then it is to be deferred to another time until the spirit manifests itself again, having left there holy water and the cross, because by the occult judgment of God, it reveals itself to certain good people and not to all. Nor is it to be feared that that spirit might harm such a person in the body if it is a good spirit, because this is not experienced as I believe sometimes. For it is already outside the state of meriting or demeriting, nor can it sin anymore, but is in a middle state between the good and the bad, certain of its predestination, but still in a state of satisfaction, namely in pains for a time. We read that the bad were punished by the bad, just as in Tobias concerning the seven husbands whom the demon Asmodeus killed, Tobias 3. Also the bad by the good, just as concerning the Sodomites whom the angels destroyed through sulfur and fire, as is evident in Genesis. Also the good by the bad, just as Job by Satan. But we do not read that the good were punished by the good unless for their own salvation, just as it served as a medicine for them, just as Zechariah by the angel Gabriel, who deprived him of the office of the tongue, Luke 1. And Jacob, through the touch of the angel, limped when he touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered for the sake of the custody of chastity, as is evident in Genesis. And Paul, through the angel of Satan, was buffeted by a thorn of the flesh, as he himself testifies. But if such a spirit were to harm anyone in the body, it would already be suspected that it is not one of the good but of the reprobate, saving divine judgment.

Another is the key of excellence which Christ has as man, and such he could communicate to ministers or priests, who are "dispensers of the mysteries of God." And the priests use that key not lost by Christ in the administration of the sacraments of the new testament. And thus the truth is saved in both, that is, God alone forgives sins by the key of authority, priests by the key of ministry. This is the summary of the blessed Thomas, Part III, q. 54, art. 1 and 4. With which Thomas of Argentina agrees in the fourth book, dist. 18. And he puts the example of a prince who has the principal authority of opening and closing a castle or city; through this, however, he does not exclude the porter to whom he has entrusted the keys. He puts another example: an Emperor gives his officials the power to punish evildoers; if, however, they seek pardon and he does this or that, he releases them free; there the officials have the power of the ministry, the prince the power of excellence. So it is concerning Christ and the priests. Christ has the key of excellence in that he uses this key immediately by the merit of his most sacred passion, by this not excluding the ministry of the priests; therefore he said: "Whatever you bind upon earth will be bound also in heaven." Therefore, in confession, much guilt is forgiven and also penalty. And if it is objected that all guilt is forgiven in contrition, therefore the priest does not forgive any. It is answered that there is no true and sufficient contrition without a firm purpose of showing, from the definition of contrition, since the precept of God and the tradition of the Church bind one to confession. Likewise, if it is said that venial sins are forgiven by the sprinkling of blessed water, and by general confession, etc., it is answered according to Saint Thomas, this is as to guilt by reason of the annexed contrition, not as to the whole penalty.
