through iron and ignited scourges, I received harsh and intolerable discipline. It was such that no bronze vessel could withstand it, but rather it would dissolve into the smallest of powders. And since God could not save me by justice, nor would He damn me by mercy, He ordered me to return to the body, so that by example and word I might teach the living what penalties are owed to sinners. Afterwards, it is impossible to describe how much penance a man needs. Behold, this religious man, dying confessed and contrite, was punished thus for sins of levity, which today are reckoned as nothing. And God manifested this for our sake. How many penalties must we believe other souls also sustain, which He could have made public? For he is neither the first nor the last.

Likewise, let another religious man teach us how we can escape these pains of <term>purgatorium</term> <gloss>purgatory</gloss>. This man saw in his dreams that an account of his sins was being demanded of him most terrifically. To his inquiry as to what he was obligated for, the response was: one hundred pounds of gold. Not that he had defrauded anyone of this, but noting the measure of the penalties. He subjected himself to grave penance and to vile and abject works for three continuous years, such that he suffered tribulations from everyone. And then in his dreams he saw that he was released from ten talents. And still remaining with greater labor and ignominy, he began to feign madness and stupidity among the brothers. Therefore, the brothers began to impose even graver and more horrible works upon him, which he suffered with joy for four years. Then, in his dreams, he saw angels coming to him who pronounced him absolved of everything. And he said, "When the brothers troubled me gravely, ridiculed me, and confounded me, I remembered the debt, and I bore it graciously and manfully." And another, seeing a certain brother laughing, said to him, "Before God and the angels we are to render an account, and you are laughing?" I promise you that I will do all of that. ¶ That, however, you will look to by your prudence, by what reason you provide well for your fortunes and my name. Farewell.

<note>Large decorative drop cap 'A' in red and brown ink, featuring a central circular geometric motif surrounded by foliate patterns.</note>
An arduous cause impelled me to write to you at this time. For when I heard that you were occupied with the greatest matters, I would have deferred my business to another time, had it not been of such a nature that, if neglected by me, it could not be corrected by the counsel or aid of any other man afterward. You will bear with me, therefore, if I have interrupted you when you are agitating the greatest matters. I think you remember what words Tiro used when we both met him on the day before the Kalends of March. For when he affirmed that he was returning to grace with me with a good mind, and said that no remnants of hatred remained in him, you ordered me not only to be of an equitable mind but also to be confident and not to suspect anything further about you. I, however, by holding great faith in his words and your authority, had put away and deferred from my mind every memory of the injuries and insults that had been between us. What followed from that, you will hear better from this man whom I send to you, to whom I gave not only letters but also commands which he might bring to you concerning this matter. For after you departed from us, things (as you thought) being composed between me and him, Saturninus arrived, who (as you know) is the most seditious of all; he disturbed everything and stirred up such hatred that my fortune has never been in a worse place. For (as it is wont to be said of a disease) that evil recrudesces sometimes more harshly than it began, which can be cured by no other doctor than by you yourself. Wherefore, if you wish me to be safe, if you wish my fortunes to be whole, take care that you fly to us; there is need of speed, lest I be directed to where at no time—I do not say I may be able to be helped—but not even salvation itself, if it wished, could extract me. Farewell.

to hate this man, or allow him to be deserted. For there is no association for me with him; he was my associate and friend as long as he was of any use to our republic, but when he began to think poorly of public interests, I judge that man no differently than I ought. But that you write that you followed my counsel in this matter, I rejoice vehemently, and I exhort you so much about it that there is nothing to which I could exhort you with greater zeal. For since I had previously owed the greatest thanks to you for many offices toward me, I now owe you even greater ones, since the republic ought to be dearer to each of us than private matters. Farewell.

<note>An ornamental red initial 'M' with internal white scrollwork decoration on a plain background.</note>
I owe great thanks to your nature, since there is nothing for which I should distrust my cause. For since you are endowed with the highest prudence in judging matters (I see it cannot happen that—which happens to please many—the very obscurity of our laws would delay your sentence). You will see what is fitting for your wisdom. I, however, have the public tablets, witnesses, and other attached documents that are wont to be requested in such lawsuits so prepared that I may be judged by you to fight not with cavils (the men who flatter me recently) but with the truth itself. Farewell.

<note>An ornamental red initial 'D' decorated with white flourishes and scrollwork.</note>
Concerning the aids about which you wrote to me, your cause is instructed; there is nothing that I would cease to be doubted by you. For I (as much as it will pertain to me) will provide that no inconvenience may come to you by my negligence. It will be yours to see that, since you have an excellent cause, you may not appear to have failed yourself, and that you come after the matter is judged, lest some silence befall you by those who come into counsel about past things and, after the storm, think by what reason they could have met the dangers that are already past. I wished to write these things to you so that I might lighten your mind of that solicitude by which (as I know) you were much afflicted. Farewell.

<note>A large, decorative red initial 'H' marks the beginning of this section.</note> I give thanks to you, and great ones indeed, that you have freed me from the greatest solicitude and annoyance. But with no less pleasure did it affect me that you wrote to me about my patron, a most modest and eloquent man. For I am delighted greatly by his praise and his most magnificent duty. For even if I had never doubted about my case, which could not have been given against me in a lawsuit, yet because in judgments, no differently than in navigating, a danger often threatens, and the one who is the pilot is skilled in his art, I was always fearing lest the equity of the case, or some other fortune, might not have had that which I desired. I rejoice, therefore, that I have drawn such an orator, in whom neither human eloquence nor study was lacking. Soon (as I hope) I will congratulate him myself. Meanwhile, signify to him that I hold great gratitude for his studies and duties. Farewell.

<note>A large, decorative red initial 'V' marks the beginning of this section.</note> You desire that it be signified by me what everyone—both your friends and your fellow citizens—feels about you. There is one opinion: that no one among your equals is greater in talent, but that they fear greatly lest you do not use it sufficiently modestly. Therefore, my Antonius, if good fame delights you, if you sustain the opinion of men which is certainly not small now, see that you do not affect your other virtues, which are great, only with modesty. I understand indeed that you will be a supreme citizen in our city if you know how to use your talent modestly. Which, so that you may do, I ask again and again. Farewell.

<meta>continues from previous page: ...to be witnesses of our love. Whether you have stood in judgment regarding my necessary man, I neither chide nor accuse. For I know this was done by you for a most honest reason. I believe you alone among all others. For I know your modesty and the old custom of your prudence. If anything has been said against my necessary man in this matter, I wish you to know that it has displeased me in every way. You will see what pertains to your duty. I, however, will not change my judgment of you. Farewell.</meta>

<note>A red decorative initial Q starts the text.</note> You ask me to know in what state our affairs are. The main point is that even if all had sworn to our destruction, we could hardly be in a worse position. For we are afflicted by wars, not only foreign ones, but even (which is most detestable) civil and internal ones. Enemies roam the fields. Fields are plundered everywhere. Rural areas burn in the midst of hostility. Men are killed. Meanwhile, among my own fellow citizens, it goes badly. He who serves the public interest is considered guilty. Everyone wants to be first in the city. There is no shame. There is no reverence for the laws in the city. Already the citizens prepare for civil strife. There is no evil that remains except captivity itself, which would subject us all to the enemy's sword and servitude. Indeed, it has reached the point that I judge death itself to be the least of evils. You see what the fortune of our fatherland is, which would be somewhat more tolerable if hope had not already abandoned us all. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial A starts the text.</note> Although a sinister rumor regarding your affairs had been brought to me, I did not think that all things had been ruined among you. More things have come to me than I could have imagined. If all things have fallen against you from foreign enemies, and the tumult of war roars and surrounds your walls, all must be endured and borne with strength, as they threaten you from those quarters. But that seems to me more miserable, which you wrote to me concerning the sedition and hatreds of the citizens. This is a matter that does not proceed from counsel and authority.

<note>A decorative red initial 'N' marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> There is nothing that would be done more willingly than to inform you of the great and most beautiful things that are happening here. For after our city was freed from hostile fear and gave itself to leisure and peace, it is incredible how the state of the Republic began to be reformed and renewed day by day. If there were old discords among our citizens, they were all taken away and lifted. The leaders of the city are entering into new affinities. The fortresses which had been made to yield to the force of wars are being restored with greater care than before and with greater resources, nor were they ever in such value. Very many ancient laws and old statutes which had been neglected are now renewed by our insolence and negligence, and the approval of almost all common offices has been given, by which, if it is obeyed, no one doubts that we may see ourselves somewhat happier in this city (for such is the state of our city) than we have experienced in the long calamity and forced by fortune, which if it had found the same state on which we were relying, and peace, would have been found. I am therefore happy to make all this known to you, so that you who have been most attentive to the hope of our glory may not be ignorant of our happiness at this time. Farewell.

<note>A decorative red initial 'O' marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> I received great pleasure in my mind from the things you wrote to me. For since I had stood in constant fear, because there was long doubt about your safety, you freed me from great trouble when I learned from your previous letter that your city was freed from the siege that was oppressing it. That letter, however, affected me with such great joy because you announced to me that not only were you exempt from the highest danger, but also the Republic itself is taking on some new form and a happier state day by day. I rejoice, indeed, and more than could be believed, that I am happy for your happiness. I certainly see those excellent foundations of your ancestors' Republic being excited by you with great study. For since the laws in which the safety of your city was placed had come into your forgetfulness, and the ancient custom was not being kept in the city, it was no wonder if your country was led to a siege. But now with laws restored and all good custom repeated, I hope your city will be wider and more opulent.

to the divine powers. If, however, the fates cannot be bent by any peace of ours, we will enjoy the good that those who understand in their own adverse affairs that nothing was omitted by them. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'M' marks the beginning of this paragraph.</note> Our army has attained the greatest praise of all on this day. It stood so firmly in battle array against the enemies that, by persisting in dying for the defense of the country, it brought back the most famous victory from there. That huge fear and the trembling fame of the whole city are removed from us. For where we expected the worst, namely to be crushed by a long siege, we have attained an unexpected victory, which in the war it certainly seemed to us that heaven itself and all the divine powers had fought on our behalf. For such was the outcome of this great affliction that hardly any of our soldiers fell in the war. What fortune the other side had is apparent from this, that they all were as if cattle, ready to be killed. Twenty military standards were captured; the camps of the enemies were completely broken and plundered. Nor was that battle one which was not received by the edge of the sword, or accepted by our forces. But when our victorious army returned to the city, adorned with very many and great trophies of the enemies, our entire city was poured out to the spectacle in a wonderful way. There was truly no one who was not giving praise and thanks to God. The wealthy, however, were praising not as a human matter, but as divine. Indeed, such was the joy and exultation of all that it seemed no longer the faces of many people, but one face and one mind. Truly, no man's house was not open to all. Everywhere our militia was received with such generosity and such abundance of everything that there was never a greater amount, even in the highest fertility of the fields. I wanted all these things to be known to you, so that you who were an ally in our dangers might also become a participant in the public tranquility and might rejoice in our fortunes. Farewell.

sample.seedTranslation: <note>A red decorative initial 'E' marks the beginning of the text.</note> I received your letter full of new things. It grieves me that the state of so many magnificent cities and peoples is coming to this. For since in all Latium there is none more illustrious from arms, I see that that ancient glory of Cisalpine Gaul has now almost faded away, reduced to desolation. Oh, fortune has this of the greatest of all things, that when it has reached the summit, then we realize it is at its end. Greece itself (if I may repeat the examples of the ancestors a little further) for a long time not only in disciplines but also in arms conquered Italy; nor was it far from possessing the empire of the orb of lands under the leader Alexander. This having been taken away from human affairs, Greece itself failed. Rome, I want as an example of all the Punic wars and nations, in the name of the empire which it had surpassed from the kings, under the solar empire which it extended to the Parthians, under the emperors, I want not only fame but also its power to have flowed with the boundaries of the world, yet it could not save or protect that empire which had once been donated. Hear this of all its glory, through the change of customs in Greece, it is long since transferred by external kings, sometimes to the West, sometimes to the North. It rejoices in this one thing, and is desolate, that there is no one of those to whom the government of our world has flowed who does not rejoice to be called the king of the Romans. Gallia, however, had grown in such a way in both the fame of its achievements and the excellence of its best men, that it seemed to conquer and surpass the splendor of the rest of the Punic affairs. Now you write to me of its ruin and end. I have no consolation by which I can better alleviate your fortune than by these examples which I also often use, since something has happened to me which is a bit harsh and bitter in my affairs. Nothing, however, is being done in this reign which should be known for its novelty or magnitude; for we are all in such leisure, how much I know not if we have been otherwise, fearing that this might perchance harm virtue itself by all our actions. <meta>continues from previous page: ...as they perceive the public interest. Since they will understand that the best men are with them, through military aid, and that those who have no doubt they will be oppressed by them for any reason are in the first place in the senate. Not that they themselves can do everything they might wish. But I do not know if I should celebrate this victory of yours with many words; I do not need much admonition to know how I might help your counsels with aid as well as with loyalty. I hope you have wisely foreseen all things that could happen on either side. It is perhaps lacking for you to have men to complete this great matter. But it is perhaps not the mark of the greatest wisdom to know how to use moderation in winning, and sometimes to stop in the middle of the course of victory, rather than to proceed further. I do not say that such a good opportunity should be neglected. For there are many things that, under this or that victory, invite them to sudden arrival: the fear of the enemy, the novelty of the deed, the loss of their own men whom you heard were almost all intercepted on those same routes. Everything is in turmoil among them; thus, it will provide easier things for you. But since fortune has a great empire in military matters, many things are to be feared by you. But I do not know if anything is more to be feared than that those who have begun to win do not attend sufficiently to the dangers. Nothing is usually done by them without rashness. But the spirit of the enemy grows internally, and the hope that had fallen at the first impetus rises greater for them. Furthermore, it sometimes happens that those who were driven into flight restore the war, and fight more sharply than if they had not despaired of victory from the beginning. I would write more about this matter if I had leisure, or if I thought your city needed advice. And it is also true that counsel should be taken about the greatest matters not after the deed is done, but before the thing happens. You, however (as you write to me), have already moved the standards to the enemy’s city. I hope that your plans find that outcome which fortune seems to me to have promised to you in the success of the fatherland. You will do a welcome thing for me if you write all things to me maturely about the outcome of your affairs. Farewell.

sample.seedTranslation:
The act of our city in which Gaius Lucius was absolved by the laws and established in that dignity is approved, which he often deserved by fighting most bravely for the fatherland. How much that matter has added to these studies of mine which I undertook for the republic, you will understand shortly; for the glory of our Gaius often excites me from sleep. I shall not rest until I see him equal to those who I judge to be his superiors in age and glory, having followed him in magnitude of mind and magnificently performed deeds. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>Not about private conveniences (as often before) but about the safety of our citizens have I signed these letters to you. If there was ever a time that the status of the republic was a care to you, see that on this day you are willing to be present to help them and your son. For a high danger hangs over them, which, unless they are managed by you most attentively, will easily erupt into a great conflagration. Wherefore, again and again, hasten to us. Nor let any matter be so great that it delays your arrival. All who are affected by your presence write that the common safety of all is placed in you alone. Do not, therefore, defer the expectation of all. Persuade yourself that it is better than any principate for a man to be loved by his citizens, and with this glory of all, that he has fled no danger or labor for the republic. You know the benevolence and hope of all the citizens placed in you; write not, you who know everything and love the fatherland greatly, as you will see these things better with yourself. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'F' marks the beginning of the text.</note>The ability, as you wish, to be able to help the republic, certainly I would flee no labor or danger for the common safety. But there are many things that strike me with diffidence and desperation regarding this matter. For many of ours prefer rather to disturb everything, so that they themselves might seem to be in charge, than to live among us with equal law, and there are many in the city who do not understand enough what is in the virtue and liberty of the citizens. If anyone, however, is found in the city who judges and feels well about the republic, his speech is of no value to the multitude. Nor do I see, therefore, what my presence can bring to the fatherland and to our citizens, unless I take upon myself many enmities, which are necessary neither for me nor for the republic. But when it will have come to the opinion that I should commit my safety to these waves and storms of the republic, I will not refuse to try everything for the love of the fatherland, rather than to fail such expectation of our citizens. You have my judgment about the republic. You, as soon as it is decided again about the will of our citizens, hasten to write to me what I am to do. Farewell.

which I know, because of your singular benevolence toward me, you will always have grieved over my adverse chances and especially rejoiced in my good things. Farewell, and write to me often about your status.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>That you have acted most humanely with him is not to be attributed to the fortune of your situation but to his own character. For you are the most pleasant of all men. I know that his witticisms and your suavity in all speech have helped you no less perhaps than if you had always been opulent in pecuniary matters. For there is a kind of men, more greedy than cruel. Since you were usually pleasant to them and did not have anything for them to gain with you, they promised for themselves, lest you should become expensive to them, so I judge the deed. As for those things which you narrate were done by them at your departure, that they not only gave you a free departure but also provisions and other offices of humanity, I cannot wonder enough, since such piety is hardly found among those men who wish to be called frugal and good. It is (as I think) that those who have long relied on the crimes of others will seek to hear honest studies, as those who live according to the laws and judgments. Whatever it may have been, I congratulate you greatly that you have freed me from maximum fear and yourself from no small danger. I desire, however, that such fortune is not to be experienced again, and you will be (as I hope) more cautious in guarding your own safety henceforth. I give thanks to God that you wrote to me first about your liberation. For you knew that I was no less anguished by your inconveniences than by my own. I urge you, however, and implore you to come to us. You will do what is most pleasing to your friends after your return, and to me, it is most pleasant, so that you could not affect me with any greater accumulated pleasure. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'R' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I write to you of an unusual matter, which you will judge to have been born from your own prudence. It will excite (believe me) a certain incredible love in you for great things. Gaius Lucius,

of <term>Caius Cornelius</term> <gloss>a name</gloss>, I follow you. For I have always seen eloquence in the cause of an orator to prevail greatly, to dominate in judgments as if in its own kingdom. But I know not how that matter will be well transacted by me. For in the matter, money is needed, and I, from the previous lawsuit, am exhausted not only in acting (which had been with me), but I am also held by great alien debt. But that I ask and beseech of you, that if you can apply any remedy for some opportunity through others, do not let any occasion pass by. I have decided that I will restore to integrity the hope of my friend, <note>or "my friend who has disappointed my hope"</note>, and that I will not let any patronage be ruined. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>My matter is in safety, and now (as they say) you are sailing into the harbor. For nothing that could be desired by friends was lacking for you for the victory of your cause. For it was fought with study and diligence so that your matter might be brought to where it finally arrived. It was God who was solicitous in this cause of yours as if it were his own, and perhaps even more, because in the cause of friends it is fitting that we be somewhat more attentive than in our own matter. You will say what thanks you owe me and your friends, not because they are ignorant of your mind, but so that your benevolence toward them may be more tenacious. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'N' marks the beginning of the text.</note>It is a bad office which I would call more necessary than that you should be grateful to those by whom we have been well received. Nor was there need for your admonition for me, because all things that are said to you always not only delight me, but I also magnify them. I was writing, therefore, to friends not to pass over that kind of thanks. For after my matter is placed in safety by their study, there is nothing that can be satisfied by me by their office. But I will make it known that I will make no end to living up to this greatest benefit of theirs. To you, truly, I give many thanks who, out of benevolence, have made me more informed than all others about these matters which I most wished to hear. Farewell.

Whatever he advises you, consider it as the saying of a truthful Apollo, as they say. If you will be willing to attend, you will see that he can neither err on account of wisdom, nor will he wish to, on account of human benevolence. I desire to understand what you will establish, so that when I have learned that you have changed from the opinion in which you have been until now, I might sufficiently congratulate our friendship. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial 'O' marks the beginning of the text.</note>I use the advice of <term>Veturius</term> <gloss>a name</gloss>. For I have always valued his wisdom highly. If I may speak with your good permission, you seem to me to feel less well about me, when you see me dissuading from using the friendship of those men whose appearance is flattering. I, however, differ from you by far. But one must live with men in such a way as the custom of each one is. I do not judge it to be that of a wise man, when others smile to themselves, for him to weep, or to be too severe when others are in jest. For I have established my life so as to accommodate myself to the matters present, nor would I suffer anyone to be angry at me rightfully. But as often as it is permitted, know that I do nothing more willingly than to spend time with those from whom I can become more learned in wisdom. These things I know have not yet been reported by my rivals. These things, as I considered them to be mine, I wrote in response to you at this time, not because I am angry at your admonitions, but so that if you had taken up a not good opinion about me, I might purge myself before you. But if anything else is carried about me, which is unworthy of my dignity and the estimation which you have of me, write all (as you do) amicably and freely. One thing I ask, allow it to be obtained from you by your humanity, that you believe nothing rashly about me. For there are many who, moved by some hatred or envy, come to impugn the fame of another, rather than being led by reason or any honest cause. If you will grant this to me, I will always be most delighted by your admonitions. Farewell.

sample.seedTranslation: <note>A red decorative initial 'S' at the beginning of the text.</note>I write to you about religion, which is the one thing that has always been judged by the wisest men to be entirely worthy of our care and our study. For neither would the Roman people have possessed a king, nor would it be called the prince of all nations and peoples, had it not placed religion above every empire and all things. And if they also cultivated what was a false religion for their own truth, I would never judge that their empire could have grown so much, or that it would have stood so long after it grew, had not all their deeds, even the smallest, been initiated first under good auspices and divine worship. What, then, is it fitting for us to judge, for whom the true and immortal religion was first invented by our ancestors, and afterwards published and accepted by us with the best reason? And this is what the Roman people learned, then Sparta and others. Who held the leadership of Greece for a long time. For they thought there was nothing that would better turn men to humanity than if they feared and revered the gods. To act well and faithfully, not a few of our emperors were true followers of the faith if they considered the affairs of peace and war. For those who for a long time referred peace and war to divine worship, all things succeeded prosperously for them, in such a way that, for their victory, often the elements and nature itself fought. Theodosius, by just opinion, is to be numbered among the clear Caesars, since he sought all wars under divine auspices, and bore the name of the one and immortal God inscribed on his standards and banners. He not only had men as aid, but he is read to have had the gods themselves as helpers. <note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> How much I cultivate all my relatives from the heart, you will easily understand if you think about my studies toward them. For everyone's own are dear to each person. But I do not think there is anyone of them whom I know who pursues his own with greater benevolence than I do mine. I cannot sufficiently admire what some men can think of me, whom neither my previous duties toward my own nor my benefits can move, and who go about disparaging me. But words (as I see) are useless to them for other things. They want to be bothersome, and they prefer to speak maliciously rather than benevolently. I have, however, in this sickness and annoyance, one great relief: that we live in a city in which we are both sufficiently known. They will not, however, effect that I should depart from my custom, and so that their eyes may crack more with pain, I will always study to be more dutiful and more kind toward my own. Whatever study can be done by me for you against such men, you will take up the whole of it through our old benevolence. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> What great annoyance I received from your letter, because your duties toward all your relatives were sufficiently seen by all the citizens. For I have never been less solicitous for your dignity than for my own. But since there is no one who does not judge most excellently of you, I think it ought rather to be guarded against—their own dignity, by those who desire to lower your good estimation from the minds of men—than that you should have to doubt about your fame. If, however, it happens that you hear otherwise about yourself, I will not bear it dissemblingly, and I will even make it so that those who came prepared to speak maliciously about another will dare much worse things about themselves. Whatever they may plot against you, there is nothing that should greatly disturb you. For the opinion which good men have formed of you is stronger than that it can be violated by such men. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial T.</note> I have cultivated friendship, which is from honesty, above all things, and I have borne nothing else in human affairs with greater regard. Now, however, it would be the most shameful thing to neglect the reason for this, whether of virtue or custom, which I have often placed before many and great things. I will tell you what reason has pushed me to this. For I have so persuaded myself that either there is no good in life, or that it is joined with friendship. If it were done for our own study, I would not admire this good so much. But since I see that all men are led and driven by nature itself to this, that they live together and love themselves, there is no one who does not judge this thing as divine. For not all come to friendship equally; but as each one is worth more in virtue and talent, so he accommodates himself to them more rightly and better. For we see that the studies of men are various: some hope for utility in friends, others for honors; some are excited to those things so that they may have those with whom they may amuse themselves. The wise man, however, places all the fruit of friendship in honesty. And I, when I had decided to love, not through good men, took care not to follow others than those I understood to be pleasing for their own sake. I was afterward so attentive in that matter that I took care of one thing: that I should not be surpassed by any of my own in duty. I will tell you what is true: I love men so that they may be pleased. I never love more than when good things happen to my friends. Even if I do not wish for bad things to happen to them, yet that seems to me the highest time for friendship: either when friends expect our effort more, or when they can love those whom they love from the heart. Those, when there is some sickness of friends, which can be healed by helping, made me besides more dutiful in friendship, because I promised myself that I could not but be loved by them, whom I loved so much, which reason has never deceived me, although I will never be wearied in the love of my own. For I hope that by these reasons I can reconcile the minds of many men to myself. For you yourself have often exhorted me to this matter. I have held your opinion as of such value that I held none more. You will therefore see, according to your wisdom...

<note>A red decorative initial Q at the beginning of the paragraph.</note> ...also all the studies of your humanity were recently inspected. I believe that you will dispel every suspicion among others. As far as I am concerned, I judge that it is promised by you what it would befit a good son to provide. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q.</note> With what mind I was toward my parents I understood in other letters, and I have never desired their presence more than after I began to excel in human affairs. For as often as I recall the memory of them, I have never since been seen to have spent a day in happiness. When I am deprived of the sight and conversation of them, I cannot easily say whether I am happier because I have had such parents, or more miserable because I have lost the ornaments and aids of life through their death. But one thing most increases this my grief: that neither piety nor my own modesty can subdue crude envy and persuade them to temper their malice. Since after this neither the human casualties that occur to all men, nor any shame or reverence for nature can inhibit them, let them remain among those joys, while I am afflicted nights and days by the desire for them, so that they may one day understand what it is to lose those who ought to be dearer to us than our own lives. I do not think there is anyone (unless by chance someone happens to be similar to such men) who would not prefer to abound in wealth and other goods without care, rather than with them amidst labor and annoyance. For I have never understood (if I may speak for myself) while those best parents of mine were living, that there was any annoyance or anxiety. Never, since they passed from life, have I spent one entire night without any interruption of rest. And it is this which troubles me vehemently, when it is thrown in my face by them that I, out of greed for wealth, rejoiced at the death of my parents by my own will. One thing only makes the insult of my detractors easier to bear: that I have you as my highest friend, inferior to no one of these citizens in authority or virtue, whom I do not doubt can most easily overcome the speeches and malice of these men.

<note>A red decorative initial S marks the beginning of the text.</note> I praise and admire your solicitude and the zeal which you used in this matter of mine. I myself, even more so, <note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> will use it for you. It delights me. For I see nothing that can be added to this benevolence of yours toward me. I wish I could give thanks. To return them in deed someday. If you are pleased with this, I would wish it. The memory of your benefits toward me will be everlasting. For as much as I can be moved in my soul, I will accomplish so much that I will think of no thing more often than how I may always do those things which I understand you want and expect. Otherwise, I will assign it to fortune or to my own imprudence if I do not seem to satisfy as much as I ought in your immortal services toward me. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial L marks the beginning of the text.</note> In all business which I know pertains to you, I will give all my labor, care, and zeal. And let this be written by me, that I wish that no gratitude be owed by you to me, which by your merit is already long since given. For you have deserved so well of me that there is nothing that I would hesitate to undertake for you or to accomplish for you. If there is anything in your affair that can be done by me, you will receive it as already done, not in advance. Think that there is no thing so arduous that I would not think it to be very easy, as long as I understand that some duty of mine can be of service to you. See, therefore, that you write to me often about all your affairs, and do not permit me to be idle. For I will think that I am loved by you the most when you have imposed some great thing that is in your interest upon me often. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> That you write to me about your love is customary, and already ancient. For when was there a time in which you did not value my affairs more than your own? For I receive pleasure from the fact whenever I hear something of your benevolence. that I might be able to return gratitude to you. I hope you will understand that nothing has been undertaken by me at any time with greater zeal than to prove by deed the gratitude which I have eternally for you. If you learn of anything in which my work can be of benefit to your own, allow it to be obtained by you, so that as you used my service for Appuleius recently, you may wish to use me for all your affairs as is your right. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> I would not have thought that the zeal and care which I undertook for your safety could be increased in you. It is incredible how much every single day adds to my love for you. For since I began to love you, there has been no time in which I did not think of you at length and have conversation about you. If at any time I meet any of your relatives, with whom I wish to recount what prudence and humanity you possess, I feel my love for you doubled, and my benevolence toward you increased far more than can be believed. For as often as I consider in my mind your kindnesses to me, which are daily greater, that thing brings so much to my original love that I now cherish you more than my own eyes. Therefore, I set no limit to loving you. Nor is there anything I think of more than that I may seem grateful enough to you and to men. But your merits in me are so great, and the heap of your benefits so large, that I do not say to return gratitude, but not even to say enough (in my judgment) could I be equal to you. That, however, you will consider more for your nature than for my merit, with what affection and benevolence, not by what means, I am prepared with a great soul and zeal to return the owed gratitude to you. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial N marks the beginning of the text.</note> You are too obliging to me, and of too grateful a spirit, when you attribute more to my benefits toward you than I recognize as being attributable to me. For there is no time in which you have not brought greater gratitude than you had previously received from me

at the same time it took away his counsel. They can write to you that everything must be attempted by you. From whom you should depart. Farewell.

<note>A red decorative initial Q marks the beginning of the text.</note> In what state I have been, and in what I am placed, I do not think you are ignorant. But that which disturbs me most is that I have neither the spirit nor the counsel by which I can help myself. For I was instituted by nature such that I could not dissimulate my grief, nor was I educated under such precepts that I could patiently bear my poverty. You know how softly I was nurtured by my parents. I could never have hoped to be brought to this indignity, that I should fall from those resources which, earned by great virtue, could have benefited all good citizens. But fortune has deceived my counsels, and it has unexpectedly cast down that most flourishing state of mine in which I long lived happily. For I believed there was at some time an end to these adversities, and (as is said in a trite proverb) that time removes sickness from men. I truly see, however, that I am experiencing what is false. For in the anger of fortune it always recrudesces, and the longer I am in conflict with these discomforts and molestations, the more I feel I am deteriorating. Shame, however, primarily stands in my way. For if I happened to show myself to my friends, or if I confessed my want, much aid would come from them. Such confusion holds my mind that I would rather perish in want than reveal my poverty. You know what it is for a man not ignoble, and who is of a noble spirit, to beg from another. I could scarcely even be induced to give these letters to you, who are most familiar to me. But your faith and benevolence have dispelled all my hesitation. You, for the sake of our friendship, will see again and again if there is anything in which you can help me among our friends. That, indeed, I am prohibited from doing by too much modesty. Farewell.

I wished for nothing less than that at that age in which you are, you would announce so many evils. That those things were to come to you, I could never have persuaded myself. For when I recall my memory, you have never harmed anyone, but you have been of help to many either by counsel or by your resources. I most marvel if you can bear this contumely of fortune with a sufficiently steady spirit. For who would not bear it most molestedly, that after many labors, at that age, he experiences all the most turbulent things, which ought to be a harbor of all rest and tranquility? I am truly compassionate, and at times I bear the indignity of this your calamity more bitterly than you, and would bear it more molestedly, if I did not recognize in you that virtue which brings you sufficient protection. But though I desire to demonstrate what spirit you are of, I truly learned that same thing most of all from your letters. For judging correctly, you think no evil ought to appear great which is about to be temporary. If there is anything which brings bitterness to anyone's spirit, I think it is that the evils which happen to us were not expected. Although by your wisdom I judge that there was no time in which you did not foresee that nothing in these things exists that is firm or stable. Use, therefore, these remedies at this time, which you practiced many years before. What of my counsel shall I bring? I have none, since I myself have always used yours in all my affairs. I offer you my fortunes, labors, and myself freely. And this I most wish you to ask of me, that you count everything among your goods.

How heavy it is for me in old age to serve near poverty. You can easily make an estimate from yourself and others. But it does not matter to me, because you are accustomed to poverty; I, however, since I have always lived in the splendor and abundance of fortune, cannot bear that yoke. If, however, a single ecclesiastical or worldly person has done this, he incurs the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term> <gloss>by the fact itself</gloss>, from which no one is absolved unless restitution of the aforesaid has been made, except at the article of death.

¶ The nineteenth principal has two. First, if anyone of those, as above, has come to the Roman curia openly or secretly and has departed from the curia without the license of the lord Pope, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. Second, if anyone knowingly has received a bishop, as above, lurking near the Apostolic See, or has not taken care to make manifest to the lord Pope or to anyone through whom the notice could be led to him, the reception and arrival of those, he is excommunicated <term>ipso facto</term>. These two cases are had in the constitutions of <term>Joh. XXII</term> and <term>Platon. r. c.</term>, <term>Et si doceat</term> <gloss>And if it teaches</gloss>. ¶ The twentieth principal case is confirmed from the Council of Constance by Martin, there in the bull <term>Multo</term> <gloss>Much</gloss>, and in these words: We order them to be suspended by that very fact. Elections, postulations, and confirmations, and whatsoever petitions simoniacally made of churches, monasteries, dignities, personages, offices, and ecclesiastical benefices are null by the law itself, and no right is acquired by them to anyone, nor does the promotion or petition produce its fruits, but those receiving them are held to their restitution as if they were unjustly given; and the givers and receivers incur the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term>, even if they shine with pontifical or cardinal dignity. ¶ The twenty-first: this is from the Council of Basel 12. Thus, those simoniacally elected or pontiffs or abbots, and those who were the principals of this simoniacal election, and those choosing and confirming, in the horror of such a penalty, incur the sentence of excommunication <term>ipso facto</term>; nor can those elected and confirmed be absolved from such guilt and excommunication unless they freely resign the churches and dignities to which they were shamefully assumed, and they remain perpetually rendered unable to obtain those which they acquired through wicked ingress. ¶ Concerning the cases touching principally religious men and women. ¶ Chapter five.

sample.blockSeed: ¶ The fifteenth principal: one who in the city or diocese of another, while exercising the office of a vicar or prelacy, intrudes himself against the form of the decree <term>De officiis ordinis</term> <gloss>On the offices of the order</gloss> and <term>In plerisque</term> <gloss>In many cases</gloss>. Rarely does this case happen, whence if someone, without the bishop's invitation, wishes to exercise episcopal functions or carry the cross outside the province, he seems to fall into it. ¶ The sixteenth principal is against those who are summoned to direct nuns in their elections, unless those thus summoned abstain from these, through whom discord could arise among them regarding the making of elections, <term>Extra de electionibus</term> <gloss>On elections</gloss>, chapter <term>Indempnitatibus</term> <gloss>On indemnities</gloss>, Book 6. And <term>Pe. Pa.</term> says: Note that in this case the advocate falls who, out of love of profit, studies to appeal against the canonically elected, if he does not advise well. ¶ The seventeenth principal contains three cases. The first is against those who, regarding the constitution of Nicholas IV, <term>De verborum significatione</term> <gloss>On the meaning of words</gloss>, <term>Exiit</term> <gloss>He went out</gloss>, Book 6, made regarding the understanding and exposition of the rule of the blessed Francis of the Friars Minor, have presumed to gloss it by explaining the approval of others grammatically. <term>Joh. An.</term> <gloss>Johannes Andreae</gloss> says: I think it is necessary that an impediment precedes and a warning follows. The second is against doctors or readers who have taught in public, from certain knowledge and deliberately, perverting the understanding of that constitution. The third is against those making any writings or booklets and, from certain knowledge and deliberately, determining in schools or preaching against those things which are contained in the aforesaid constitution. It is to be noted also by <term>Joh. XXI</term> in the constitution <term>Quia nonnunquam</term> <gloss>Because sometimes</gloss>, that the sentences and penalties laid against the glossators of Nicholas IV's <term>Exiit qui seminat</term> <gloss>He went out who sows</gloss> are suspended until the good pleasure of the Apostolic See. Through such suspension, he does not intend to give license to teach, write, determine, preach, or speak privately against the rules of those Friars Minor, publicly or secretly. ¶ The eighteenth principal is in the constitution of <term>Joh. XXI</term>, <term>Suscepti regiminis</term> <gloss>Of the government undertaken</gloss>, as follows: If anyone has taken from the fruits of a benefice, from which the first year's fruits or others are owed to the fabric or church of some person, beyond the portion taxed by the lord Pope John, and has not restored it to him to whom it pertains within a month with effect: if he is a bishop or superior, he is suspended from the entrance of the church and from pontificals. If, however, it was a chapter or a university or a college, they are interdicted until they have restored the aforesaid in full.

sample.seedTranslation: The fifth principal is concerning the immunity of the church and those who, holding temporal dominion by license of anyone, forbid their subjects to sell anything to prelates or clerics or ecclesiastical persons, or to buy anything from the same, or not to grind grain for them, bake bread, or show them other services, is not bound, says the said Pope, except for dukes and prelates. The sixth principal is against those who from churches and ecclesiastical persons, for their own proper goods which they carry or cause to be carried, not for the sake of trading, demand or extort tolls <term>pedagia</term> <gloss>road or bridge tolls</gloss> or suchlike by themselves or others in their name or another, or compel them to pay such, a contrary custom notwithstanding; and the bishop of the place ought to publish them as excommunicated, or cause them to be published by his subjects, until they have restored what was thus exacted and have satisfied for such transgression competently, <term>Extra de censibus</term>, chapter <term>Quaestione</term>, Book 5, § <term>Qui vero</term>, nor do they excuse, says the said Pope, at the time from which memory exists, clerics paying tolls, which the Pope understands of ancient tolls, not of new ones. The seventh principal case contains two. The first: that laymen who formerly through force or fear compelled prelates or the chapter of churches or other ecclesiastical persons to submit to them immovable goods or rights of churches without the consent of the chapter and the license of the Pope, unless they relax such submissions after the requisitioning warning. And that henceforth they compelled prelates or other ecclesiastical persons to do such things. The second: whoever through submission rightly made until now usurps anything beyond that which is permitted by licit tract, unless they desist from such usurpation having been lawfully warned, and restoring also what they have usurped, <term>Extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis</term> <gloss>On not alienating church goods</gloss>, and this in the newest § <term>Laici</term>, Book 6. The eighth principal has two. The first is against those who, under the title of royal custody or guard of their advocacy or defense, attempting to usurp anew in churches, monasteries, or other pious places, presume to usurp the goods of the same churches, monasteries, or pious places that are vacant. The second is against clerics, monks of monasteries, and persons of churches of the same places that allow this to be done, <term>Extra de electione</term>.

Quintus principalis est de immunitate ecclesiae et eos qui licentia quorumcunque obtinentes temporale dominium subditis suis interdicunt ne praelatis aut clericis seu personis ecclesiasticis quicquam vendant aut emant aliquid ab eisdem vel ne ipsis blada molant panem coquant aut alia obsequia eis exhibeant non est ligat dicto papa nisi duces et praelates. Sextus principalis est contra illos qui ab ecclesiis et personis ecclesiasticis pro rebus suis propriis quas non causa negotiandi deferunt vel deferri faciunt pedagia seu huiusmodi talia exigunt vel extorquent per se vel alios suo nomine vel alieno aut eos ad huiusmodi soluenda compellunt contraria consuetudine non obstante et debet episcopus loci publicare ipsos excommunicatos vel a suis subditis facere publicari donec sic exacta restitueret et de transgressione huiusmodi satisfecerit competenter extra de censibus et quaestione libro quinto § qui vero nec exculant dicto papa qua tempore a quo extat memoria clericos pedagimat quae de antiquis pedagis papa intelligit non de novis. Septimus casus principalis orinet duos. Primus quod laici qui quondam per vim vel per metum opellebant praelatos vel capitulum ecclesiarum seu alias personas ecclesiasticas sibi submittere bona immobilia vel iura ecclesiarum absque consensu capituli et licentia papae nisi post repetente ammonitionem huiusmodi submissiones relaxet. Et quod de cetero praelatos vel alias personas ecclesiasticas ad talia facienda compulerit. Secundus quicunque per submissionem rite hactenus facta aliquid usurpat ultra id quod ex tractu licito pmititur nisi legitime moniti ab huiusmodi usurpatione destiterit et restituendo etiam quae talia usurpavit extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis et hoc novissimo § laici libro sexto. Octavus principalis habet duos. Primus est contra illos qui regalia custodia vel guardia advocatonis suae seu defensionis titulo in ecclesiis monasteriis seu aliis piis locis de novo usurpare conantes bona eorundem ecclesiarum monasteriorum seu piorum locorum vacantium usurpare praesumunt. Secundus est contra clericos monachos monasteriorum et personas ecclesiarum eorundem locorum quae fieri id permittit extra de electione.

Quomodo confessor seipsum disponere debet ad eum qui sibi confitebitur dantur desuper duodecim regule. ¶ Cap. primum.

Secunda pars nunc incipit de necessariis confessionem concomitantibus. in quo ut confessor officium gerit medici morbos animi facilius sanare valeat. in applicando sacramento penitentie septem capita sequentia incorporat. ¶ Primum quo ad confitentes bene disponendos se preparare debeat. ¶ Secundo qua ab ipso confitente gnaliter querere habeat. ¶ Tercio que vitia luxurie de quibus magna vis est a verecundia specialiter rimari valeat. ¶ Quarto quo circa fines confessionis reu corrigere deceat informare atque per que confessum esse veritum vel attritum nosse expediat. ¶ Quinto que iter penitentia vel satisfactio debite iniungat. ¶ Sexto quo rite a peccatis a sententiis absoluat. ¶ Septimo quo circa infirmos caute se teneat et celato confessionis. Quo ad primum ante confessionem et circa eam exordium xii. sequentes regulas attendat. ¶ Prima ut auctoritate super confitente habeat seu iurisdictionem is alienus vult confessionem audire. puta pape. epi plebani vel ut sit prelate? epo rite si e de ordine medicantium Frater. potest enim subditus in octo casibus alteri quam proprio sacerdoti confiteri vel alteri quam prius fuit ei sacerdos proprius. Primum quando proprius sacerdos est omnino indiscretus et inscius. et ab eo est licentia petita licet non obtenta. vel debet saltem a superiori proprii confessoris seu sacerdotis licentia peti si haberi potest. Secundo quando parochianus transtulit domicilium suum. tunc iste est subditus illius sacerdotis ad cuius parochiam se transtulit. Tercio quando quis querit domicilium quo se conferat. quia sine domicilio est. Quarto quando quis est vagabundus. Quinto si est in studio de licencia prelatorum suorum. Sexto si est peregrinus qui recipit peram et baculus a proprio sacerdote aut eius vicario vel licenciam vel si est mercator aut viator. et recipit licenciam a proprio sacerdote. secus autem si peregrinus vel mercator vel viator prefata non fecerit.

The first against those who presume to capture Christians navigating for the sake of trade or for other honest causes, or to despoil them of their goods. The second is against those who despoil Christians suffering shipwreck of their goods. And Petrus de Palude notes that in the first case he says here "honest causes," because of pirates and those who carry forbidden things to the Saracens and otherwise lead many wars at sea; other thieves, however, are not excommunicated. Therefore princes and others who receive the goods of shipwrecked persons cannot be excused, since it is against all equity and even natural law. He adds, however, in the letter where above to the cases: unless they return the stolen goods after warnings, or after they have been in delay, since they can restore and do not restore. ¶ The second is introduced against powers, consuls, and rectors and other officials, laymen of cities and other places, imposing burdens <term>angarias</term> <gloss>mandatory services</gloss> and undue exactions on churches, priests, and their possessions, or other burdens of their own, whether ditches or expeditions, or anything else they deem to be done, wishing almost everything to be accomplished from the goods of the churches, clerics, and the poor of Christ deputed. The second against those who succeed to the aforementioned first, unless within months they have purged the errors or excesses of their predecessors, <term>De immunitate ecclesiae</term>, § <term>final</term>, and the same, <term>Non minus</term>. ¶ The third principal has eight cases. The first is against those who hereafter have edited statutes against the liberty of the church, unless they have deleted them from the capitulars or from their cartularies or other books of theirs within two months. sample.seedTranslation: The fourth rule: it is expedient that the confessor obtain for his power from the prelate of his subjects in reserved cases, beyond, or relievers, especially unless there are public and scandalous cases. For very few are found, as the Chancellor <note>Jean Gerson</note> says from there, who have not fallen into some such case that they do not reserve; they indeed, confessors knowing themselves not to be able to be remitted henceforth to another, they detect all things more freely. The confessor indeed presumes to question them more freely and to heal more fully by absolving them once; for what else is it to remit a penitent from judge to judge in hidden things, than to add affliction to the afflicted? Certainly many existing in filth cause more causally or occasionally and become dirtier. Christ did not do so to the Samaritan, of whom Isaiah prophesies thus: he will not crush the bruised reed, and he will not extinguish the smoking flax; he will lead judgment in truth; he will not be sorrowful nor turbulent. ¶ The fifth rule: according to Hubert <note>Hubert of Romans, author of instruction manuals for confessors</note> in his book on the instructions of officials, in the chapter on the hearing of confessions: let him obtain such a place for sitting that he can be seen by many, especially when he hears women, and that the confession cannot be heard by anyone, in which he certainly provides for the fame of both himself and the one confessing. For the confessor is an angel of the Lord of the armies of God, as Malachi says, and concerning the confessor and the one confessing, Christ says: he who does truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, which were done in God. So also the blessed <term>Jerome</term> informs Nepotian: all suspicions, he says, and whatever can probably be feigned, let it be avoided by you; abstain from all bad appearance, the Apostle commands. ¶ The prelates, however, who submit these rules, easily succumb to suspicion concerning women, says Job: the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness; for, as Hubert says, if some great persons of the male sex wish to confess, of whom the confessor believes that he might be ashamed in the aid of others, he ought to lead them to another place more secret and honest.

Primus quod considerando se esse debere dei angelum et dei tremetis in iudicio vicarium. deinde a versu vel clausu ad feminas oculis corporis aie apprie lumina videat aias solaz seie ad dei insignia ymagine leprosam seu sauciatam esse diris demonum peccatorum mortalium vulneribus. vel salte seu rugosa seu scabiosa delictis venialibus quod per christi sanguinem et sacramenta poenitentiae mededuz est. Cruce occulte confessor pollice impingat peccatori suo apprio aliquntulum per puritate tuenda. brevi saltem dei invocet prece oraciuncula. et verbis sine necessitate caveat dulcibus ab oique penite? fabulatione inutili. et sic solus dei honeste et aie apprie aliene salute quere firmiet apponat. nec en desperat si teptat dum delectationi carnis renitat memor ubi christi ad discipulos dicentis. Si mortiferum quod biberint non eos nocebit. Spetes tollit etc. Super quod beatus grego. sacerdotes et bonis suis exhortationibus malicia de cordibus alienis auferunt. spetes tollunt et dum pestiferas pluaciones audiunt et en ad orationes praua perhunt. mortiferum est quod bibunt et non eos nocebit. How the confessor ought to dispose himself towards him who will confess to him; twelve rules are given from above. ¶ Chapter 1.

The second part now begins concerning the things necessary concomitant to confession, in which, as the confessor performs the office of a physician, he may be able to heal the diseases of the mind more easily; in applying the sacrament of penance, he incorporates the following seven chapters. ¶ First, how he ought to prepare himself for properly disposing those confessing. ¶ Second, what he ought to ask of the confessor himself in general. ¶ Third, which vices of lust, of which there is great force, he may be able to specifically examine regarding shame. ¶ Fourth, how he ought to inform concerning the ends of confession, what it behooves him to correct, and through what he might expedite to know the one confessing to be repentant or contrite. ¶ Fifth, what penance or satisfaction he ought to properly enjoin. ¶ Sixth, how he may rightly absolve from sins and from sentences. ¶ Seventh, how he may cautiously hold himself concerning the sick and the concealment of confession. As to the first, before confession and concerning it, let him attend to the 12 following rules. ¶ The first: that he should have authority over the one confessing or jurisdiction, if another wishes to hear the confession, for instance, the Pope, the bishop, the parish priest, or that he should be a prelate, a bishop rightly, if he is a Friar of the mendicant orders; for a subject can in eight cases confess to another than his own priest, or to another than the priest who was previously his own. First, when the own priest is entirely indiscreet and ignorant, and license is sought from him, even if not obtained, or at least license ought to be sought from the superior of the own confessor or priest, if it can be had. Second, when the parishioner has moved his domicile; then this one is a subject of that priest to whose parish he has moved. Third, when someone seeks a domicile to which he may betake himself, because he is without a domicile. Fourth, when someone is a vagabond. Fifth, if he is at a place of study with the license of his prelates. Sixth, if he is a pilgrim who receives a wallet and staff from his own priest or his vicar, or a license, or if he is a merchant or a traveler, and receives a license from his own priest; otherwise, however, if the pilgrim or merchant or traveler has not done the aforesaid.

Quomodo confessor seipsum disponere debet ad eum qui sibi confitebitur dantur desuper duodecim regule. ¶ Cap. primum.

Secunda pars nunc incipit de necessariis confessionem concomitantibus. in quo ut confessor officium gerit medici morbos animi facilius sanare valeat. in applicando sacramento penitentie septem capita sequentia incorporat. ¶ Primum quo ad confitentes bene disponendos se preparare debeat. ¶ Secundo qua ab ipso confitente gnaliter querere habeat. ¶ Tercio que vitia luxurie de quibus magna vis est a verecundia specialiter rimari valeat. ¶ Quarto quo circa fines confessionis reu corrigere deceat informare atque per que confessum esse veritum vel attritum nosse expediat. ¶ Quinto que iter penitentia vel satisfactio debite iniungat. ¶ Sexto quo rite a peccatis a sententiis absoluat. ¶ Septimo quo circa infirmos caute se teneat et celato confessionis. Quo ad primum ante confessionem et circa eam exordium xii. sequentes regulas attendat. ¶ Prima ut auctoritate super confitente habeat seu iurisdictionem is alienus vult confessionem audire. puta pape. epi plebani vel ut sit prelate? epo rite si e de ordine medicantium Frater. potest enim subditus in octo casibus alteri quam proprio sacerdoti confiteri vel alteri quam prius fuit ei sacerdos proprius. Primum quando proprius sacerdos est omnino indiscretus et inscius. et ab eo est licentia petita licet non obtenta. vel debet saltem a superiori proprii confessoris seu sacerdotis licentia peti si haberi potest. Secundo quando parochianus transtulit domicilium suum. tunc iste est subditus illius sacerdotis ad cuius parochiam se transtulit. Tercio quando quis querit domicilium quo se conferat. quia sine domicilio est. Quarto quando quis est vagabundus. Quinto si est in studio de licencia prelatorum suorum. Sexto si est peregrinus qui recipit peram et baculus a proprio sacerdote aut eius vicario vel licenciam vel si est mercator aut viator. et recipit licenciam a proprio sacerdote. secus autem si peregrinus vel mercator vel viator prefata non fecerit.

Not-obstructing, that is, who has the power to resist without his own danger and does not do it, when he is held by office to obstruct, if in this way thieves grow strong, such as are princes who by their office are held to observe justice because the rents which they have are instituted for this; they are held to make restitution. Otherwise [for those] who are not held by office to observe [justice], because they are not held to restitution.
Not-manifesting, that is, who knows where the robbed or stolen thing is [and] does not indicate it when it is requested, and when he is held to this by office, he is held to restitution; otherwise if he only knows where it is and does not indicate it, even when requested about this, [it is the case] that then one sins, yet he is not held to restitution. Whence a judge who ought to pronounce on the matter of which he knows, and thus manifest the law, if he does not do it, he is held to restitution. From the aforementioned it is also clear that any heir, whether a son or a stranger, without distinguishing the property of the robber or another, is held by canon law to pay all the debts of the deceased, whether they were from contract or quasi-contract, or from a misdeed or another [cause], whether that thing for which the debt was contracted reached him or not, whether the lawsuit was contested with the deceased or not. There is, however, a contract, such as purchase, sale, hiring, letting, loan, and similar; a quasi-contract is such as guardianship or the management of another’s affairs. A misdeed is such as theft, robbery; a quasi-misdeed is when a judge judges through incompetence, or when something is thrown or poured out from another’s house which harmed passers-by.

<margin>5</margin>
Give ear to my words, O Lady: and do not turn away the beauty of your face from me. Turn our mourning into joy and our tribulation into jubilation. May our enemies fall before our feet: by your virtue, may their heads be crushed. May every tongue bless you: and may all flesh confess your holy name. For your spirit is sweeter than honey, and your inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. **Glory.**

<margin>6</margin>
O Lady, do not let me be seized in the fury of God: nor judged in His wrath. For the honor of your name, O Lady, may the fruit of your glorious womb be propitiated toward us. From the gate of the underworld and from the belly of the abyss: by your holy prayers deliver us. May the everlasting gates be opened to us: that we may tell of your wonders forever. For not the dead, nor those in the underworld, shall praise you, O Lady: but those who shall obtain eternal life by your grace. **Glory.**

<margin>7</margin>
My Lady, in you I have hoped: deliver me from my enemies, O Lady. Close the mouth of the lion and his teeth...

### iii. Sunday.

### The Psalter of the Blessed Virgin begins, compiled by Bonaventura in honor of the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the whole human race.

<margin>1.</margin>
**B**lessed is the man who loves your name, Mary Virgin: your grace shall comfort his soul. Like an orchard irrigated by springs of water, you shall propagate the fruits of justice in him. Blessed are you among women: through the faith of your holy heart. For you surpass all women in the beauty of the flesh, you surpass the angels and archangels in the excellence of holiness. Your mercy and grace are preached everywhere: God has blessed the works of your hands. Glory be to the Father.

<margin>2.</margin>
**W**hy have our enemies raged: and meditated vain things against us? May your right hand, Mother of God, protect us like a terrible army confounding and destroying them. Come to her, you who labor and are troubled, and she shall give refreshment to your souls. Approach her in your temptations: and the serenity of her face shall stabilize you.

> is above your head: the beauty of the moon is under your feet. The twinkling stars adorn your dwelling: the constellations glorify you constantly at morning. Be mindful of us, O Lady, in your good pleasure: and make us worthy to glorify your name. Glory.

---

> **U**nto you, O Lady, have I lifted up my soul: in the judgment of God, may I not be shamed by your prayers. Let not my adversaries mock me: and those who presume to be against you shall be strengthened. May the snares of death not prevail against me, and let the camps of the wicked not impede my steps. Shatter their rush with your virtue: and come to my soul with gentleness. Be my guide to the fatherland: and deign to gather me into the assembly of the angels. Glory.

---

> **J**udge me, O Lady, for I have wandered from my innocence: but because I have hoped in you, I shall not be weakened. Burn my heart with the fire of your love: and restrain my loins with the girdle of chastity. For your mercy and your clemency are before my eyes: and I have delighted in the voice of your praise. O Lady, I have loved the beauty of your face: and I have venerated your holy majesty.

> Praise her, you heavens of heavens: and let all the earth glorify her name. Glory.
> **M**ay you hear us, O Lady, in the day of tribulation: and turn your face, full of clemency, toward our prayers. Do not cast us off in the time of our death: but succor us when the body has been abandoned. Send an angel to meet the soul: by whom it may be defended from the enemies. Show it the most serene Judge of the ages: whom you may render propitious to it for the sake of your grace. May it feel your refreshment in its punishments: and grant it a place among the elect of God. Glory.
> **F**or in your strength our heart shall rejoice: and in the sweetness of your name our soul shall be consoled. From your seat, send us wisdom: by which we may be sweetly illuminated in all truth. Grant us the grace to abstain from carnal desires: so that the light of grace may rise in our hearts. How sweet to those who love you are your words, O Lady: how sweet are the droplets of your grace. I will sing glory and honor to you: and in your name I will glory forever.
> **L**et your eye, my God, look upon me: by your merits, O ever-virgin Mary.

be to you, O Queen of heaven: and in no time do not forget us. Glory
O Lady, let not the Lord argue in his fury: by you, O best one, may there be pardon for our sins. In your sight may all our desire be: our hope and our confidence. My heart is troubled within me: the light has departed from my inwards. Illuminate my blindness with your splendor: sweeten my contrition with your sweetness. Do not abandon us, O Lady, Mother of God: let your grace and virtue be at my right hand. Hail Mary
I said I will keep my ways, O Lady: when through you the grace of Christ was given to me. My heart is liquefied by your sweetness: my inwards are inflamed by your love. Hear my prayer, O Lady, and my petition: and may my adversaries be brought to nothing. Have mercy on me from the heavens and from the height of your throne: and do not permit me to be troubled in the valley of misery. Guard my foot that it be not injured: and at my end may your grace be present. Expecting, I have expected your grace: and you have done unto me according to the multitude of your mercy.

...surround your throne. Praise her together, morning stars: make a melody for her, all you sons of God. Glorify her, heavens and earth, sea and rivers, and the foundations of the world. Glory.

<note>A red decorative initial O begins the text.</note>Deliver me from my enemies, Lady of the world: arise to meet me, Queen of piety. Adorn yourself in your ornaments: let the sardius and topaz be your diadem. Let the jasper and amethyst be your right hand: let the beryl and chrysolite be your left hand. Let the jacinth and agate be upon your breast: let carbuncles sparkle on your necklaces. Let myrrh, frankincense, and balsam be in your hands: let sapphire and emerald be on your fingers.

<note>A red decorative initial O begins the text.</note>You have turned us away because of our sins: and you have had mercy upon us through the Virgin Mary. Intercede for us, health-bringing Mother of God: for you have brought forth the salvation of angels and men. You have poured out exultation in the depths: and gladness and sweetness in your merits. Make us joyful with the sweet-flowing sound of your mouth: and pour your rosy nectar into our hearts. Thunder for her from above: and give her praise.

<summary>This passage continues a prayer to the Virgin Mary, invoking her as a celestial Queen adorned with precious stones and as a merciful intercessor who provides salvation and spiritual sweetness to humanity.</summary>

Holy Mary, solace of the afflicted, pray for us.
Holy Mary, noble Queen of the heavens, pray for us.
Holy Mary, whom the angels obey and entreat, pray for us.
Holy Mary, whom the holy saints rejoice with and congratulate, pray for us.
Holy Mary, whom all things praise and venerate, pray for us.

Be propitious. Spare us, O mistress.
Be propitious. Deliver us, O mistress.
From every evil, deliver us, O mistress. From every evil temptation, deliver us, O mistress. From the wrath and indignation of God, deliver us, O mistress. From the peril of desperation, deliver us, O mistress. From precipitous pride, deliver us, O mistress. From devastating avarice, deliver us, O mistress. From the sin of anger and the cruelty of envy, deliver us, O mistress. From the temptation of the flesh, pressing on all sides, deliver us, O mistress. From the sin of gluttony and the defilement of voracity, deliver us, O mistress. From the incursion of the malignant enemy, deliver us, O mistress. By the sweetness and joy of the incarnation of Christ, deliver us, O mistress. By the pain and anguish of His passion, deliver us, O mistress. By the joy and miracle of His resurrection, deliver us, O mistress. By your faith in the sending of the Holy Spirit, deliver us, O mistress.

sample.seedTranslation:
I did not patiently endure the injuries and insults brought upon me. ¶ For the salvation of the souls of friends and enemies, I did not pray to God, and I did not offer the reward of labor to those working for me. ¶ In whatever way I did not fulfill the works of mercy, I state my guilt and render myself culpable to God and to you.

### ¶ On the twelve articles of faith

Seventh, I sinned because I did not firmly believe the twelve articles of faith, nor did I confess them with heart and mouth for righteousness. Indeed, sometimes I doubted concerning them and concerning the sacraments of the altar. I did not have a living and just faith with good works like a good Christian, nor did I defend and preach my faith against Jews, infidels, and heretics. Indeed, I willingly listened to those wandering and arguing against the faith.

### ¶ On the seven sacraments of the Church.

Eighth, I sinned, because I passed over and neglected the seven sacraments of the Church like a good Christian. ¶ First, because although I am baptized, yet I did not renounce the devil and his pomps as I promised in baptism. And although I am confirmed, yet I blushed to speak and preach the faith of Christ and the truth for fear of the world, and I neglected it. Therefore, O pious Deity, O tremendous Majesty, I, a miserable one, caught among anxieties, run back to You, the fountain of mercy; I hasten to You to be healed; I flee under Your protection; and what I cannot endure from the Judge, I sigh to have from the Savior. To You, Lord, I show my wounds; to You, I uncover my shame. I know my sins are many and great, for which I fear. I hope in Your mercies, of which there is no number. Look, therefore, upon me with the eyes of Your mercy, pious Lord Jesus Christ, eternal King, God-man crucified for humanity. Hear me, who hopes in You, and have mercy on me, full of miseries and sins. You who will never cease to flow from the fountain of mercy. Hail, salutary victim, offered for me and all the human race on the gibbet of the cross. Hail, noble and most precious blood flowing from the wounds of my crucified Lord Jesus Christ, and washing away the sins of the whole world. Remember, Lord, Your creature whom You have redeemed with Your sacred blood. It repenteth me that I have sinned; I desire to amend what I have done.
